Proposed Proposition
This program is primarily aimed at households with moderate to higher incomes who
may not qualify for existing CalHFA programs but still struggle to afford home prices in
California.
Main Provisions – Second Mortgage Program: This measure authorizes CalHFA to
issue $25 billion in revenue bonds (separate from its existing bond authority) to fund the
"Middle-Class Homeownership Loan Program".
● Borrower Eligibility: Applicants must have been a California resident for at least
one year and earn no more than 200% of the Area Median Income (AMI) of the
county where the home is purchased.
● The Loan: Provides a secondary mortgage for up to 17% of the purchase price.
● Borrower Funds: The applicant must provide at least a 3% down payment from
their own personal funds (not a grant or other loan).
● Occupancy: The applicant must occupy the home as a primary residence within
60 days of closing.
● Property Eligibility: Limited to newly constructed homes, townhomes,
condominiums, or repurposed nonresidential units where the applicant is the first
purchaser.
● Sales Price and Loan Limit Cap: The sales price is capped at 125% of the
conforming loan limit (ranging from approx. $1M to $1.5M in 2025).
● Foreclosure Rights: The measure allows CalHFA to follow different foreclosure
procedures on these loans than those required for some private lenders.
Consumer Protections: The following consumer protections will be established:
● Lender Origination Fee: A lender may charge an origination fee of up to 0.5% or
$290, whichever is greater.
● Early Payment Penalty: No penalty can be charged for early payment of the
second mortgage.
● Fixed Rate Mortgage: The second mortgage shall be a fixed-rate mortgage."InDepth" Summaries for November 2026 Propositions

● Credit Score: If the applicant’s credit score falls below the program minimum, the
lender shall allow the applicant to submit financial records to enable “cash flow
underwriting” to qualify the applicant for more favorable terms under the program.
● Realtor/Broker: Applicant shall retain a licensed California real estate agent or
broker.
Main Provisions – Qualified Builder Option: Developers/builders can voluntarily “opt-

and builders. However, supporters and opponents may disagree on whether these
changes improve the efficiency of disputes or reduce homeowner protections.
● Builder Liability: Developer/Builder must accept full liability for all labor law

o The right to obtain a written release/waiver from the homeowner once

California’s 2026 Housing Strategy: Funding and Reform
Proposition 1 - The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026
Proposition 37 - The California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home
Construction Act of 2026
Proposition 45 - The Building an Affordable California Act
The November 2026 ballot presents voters with a multi-layered approach to the state’s
housing shortage. While they share the goal of increasing housing availability, they
function as different "tools" in the toolkit: Props 1 and 37 provide financing for different
income levels. At the same time, Prop 45 seeks to reform the regulatory process to
ensure those projects are built faster.
1. The Funding Mechanisms: Prop 1 & Prop 37
These two bond measures are complementary, as they target different populations,
provide for different housing types, and use different financial structures:
Target Populations: Prop 1 focuses on providing a mix of subsidized rental housing and
homeownership assistance for families with low incomes, farm workers, students,
veterans, and individuals experiencing homelessness, to name a few. Prop 37 assists
moderate-income households (up to 200% of Area Median Income) who earn too much
to qualify for traditional assistance programs yet are still priced out of homeownership.
Project Scope: Prop 1 funds both construction of new housing (rental and permanent)
and the preservation and rehabilitation of existing affordable housing. Prop 37 is strictly
limited to newly constructed homes to incentivize an increase in total housing supply.
Financial Impact: Prop 1 uses General Obligation bonds, which are repaid by the state
and its taxpayers via the General Fund (though the veterans' portion is intended to be
repaid through their mortgage payments). Prop 37 uses Revenue bonds, which are
intended to be self-sustaining and repaid solely by the participating homeowners,
carrying no direct cost to the state budget.
2. Removing The Regulatory “Roadblock”: Prop 45
While Props 1 and 37 provide the “fuel” (funding), Prop 45 aims to “clear the road” by
addressing the environmental, permitting, and litigation delays that supporters claim
make housing too expensive to build. Prop 45 establishes strict, mandatory time limits
for environmental reviews (CEQA) and permit approvals (PSA) for “essential projects,”
which explicitly includes the housing types funded by Props 1 and 37. Prop 45 also"InDepth" Summaries for November 2026 Propositions
League of Women Voters of California Education FundPage 32
requires courts to resolve legal challenges to essential projects within mandatory time
limits to prevent years of construction delays.
Voter Perspective
While these measures could appear complementary (in the interest of expanding
access to more affordable housing in California), critics express concern that placing
several complex housing initiatives on a single ballot may cause voter confusion or

Proposition 38 – Bonds for Research on the Immune System
Initiative Statute
The Question
Should California authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds to fund immunology
and immunotherapy research, including approximately $4.2 billion for a single nonprofit
research institute affiliated with the University of California and $4.2 billion for grants to
other California public and nonprofit universities and research institutions?
The Situation
Medical Research Funding
Medical research and development (R&D) generally moves through several stages:
1. Basic research—often conducted by universities and nonprofit research
institutions—focuses on understanding disease and developing new scientific
knowledge.
2. Applied and clinical research then evaluates potential therapies in laboratory and
patient settings before treatments can be approved for public use.
According to the Legislative Analyst's Office, private industry provides approximately
65% of U.S. medical research and development funding, while the federal government
provides about 25%. State governments play a comparatively small role in funding
medical research. Federal agencies, including the National Institutes of Health (NIH),
have historically been major sources of funding for biomedical research. Federal
funding levels and research priorities can change over time, creating uncertainty for
long-term research projects. While funding medical research has traditionally been a
federal responsibility, there remains a question of whether state taxpayers should
assume a larger role.
Immunology and Immunotherapy
Immunology is the study of the body's immune system. Immunotherapy involves
treatments that use or modify the immune system to prevent, treat, or cure disease.
Although immunotherapy is most commonly associated with cancer treatment,
researchers are also investigating its potential use in Alzheimer's disease, heart
disease, autoimmune disorders, diabetes, infectious diseases, and other chronic
conditions. California is home to numerous immunology and immunotherapy research
programs, including those affiliated with UCLA, UCSF, UC San Diego, UC Irvine,
Stanford University, and other nonprofit research institutions."InDepth" Summaries for November 2026 Propositions
League of Women Voters of California Education FundPage 36
Previous State Research Bonds
California voters have previously approved large bond measures to support biomedical
research.
Proposition 71 (2004) authorized $3 billion in general obligation bonds and created the
California Institute for Regenerative Medicine (CIRM) to support stem cell research.
This measure passed 59% to 41%.
Proposition 14 (2020) authorized an additional $5.5 billion in general obligation bonds
to continue funding CIRM. This measure passed 51% to 49%.
Unlike Props 71 and 14, which distributed funding broadly through CIRM grant
programs, this measure directs 50% of its funding to a single qualifying institute.
Supporters of these measures cite the development of research facilities, clinical trials,
biotechnology companies, workforce training programs, and medical discoveries
associated with CIRM-funded research. Studies commissioned by supporters estimated
that CIRM funding contributed to thousands of jobs and billions of dollars of economic
activity in California.
Critics note that scientific advances often take decades to develop and that direct
financial returns to taxpayers through royalties and licensing revenue have been
relatively modest compared with the overall public investment. In fact, the LAO’s
analysis of Prop 14 reported that as of 2019, CIRM grant recipients had contributed
$352,560 in total invention-related income to the state. They also point to governance
and conflict-of-interest concerns that emerged during CIRM's operation.
Unlike CIRM, which distributes funding across many institutions through a grant
process, this measure would direct half of all bond proceeds to a single research
institute while distributing the remaining funds through competitive grants.
Proposed Proposition
The California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative would authorize $8.4 billion
in state general obligation bonds, issued incrementally as funding is requested, for
immunology and immunotherapy research. The state would repay the bonds, with
interest, from the General Fund over time."InDepth" Summaries for November 2026 Propositions

● An affiliation agreement with a University of California campus
● Existence before January 1, 2025
● A specific focus on immunology and immunotherapy research
● Demonstrate significant philanthropic funding commitments
● Maintain vaccine-development and microbiome-research programs
● Control a large research facility site of specific square footage
● Include UC representatives in governance
● DPH may modify these criteria only if no institute meets the original requirements
and only to the “minimum amount of modification necessary”
The measure does not identify any institution by name, and it is unclear how many
institutions would satisfy all eligibility requirements. Some observers may note,
however, that the eligibility requirements appear similar to publicly described

nonprofit institute affiliated with UCLA that was established with substantial
philanthropic support, including funding from initiative proponent Gary K. Michelson.
Competitive Grants — 50% ($4.2 billion)
The remaining funds would be distributed through research grants to California-based
public and nonprofit universities and nonprofit research institutions. Grant funding would
support research projects in immunology and immunotherapy selected through a review

related to cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's disease. The measure also
authorizes research involving other diseases and conditions in which the immune
system is believed to play a role.
California Suppliers: Grant recipients must buy at least half of their goods and
services from California suppliers when reasonably possible

California’s Proposition 37 would let buyers put 3% down on a new home, with a state loan covering the other 17%
Proposition 37 would let CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds and lend buyers of newly built homes up to 17% of the price, so they can put 3% down. The loan is a fixed-rate second mortgage with monthly payments. Here is who qualifies, the county price caps, the cost and who is behind it.

Updated

California's Proposition 37 is asking voters to let the state lend new-home buyers up to 17% of the purchase price
Proposition 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency borrow up to $25 billion from investors and lend it to buyers of newly built homes as a second mortgage covering up to 17% of the price. The buyer puts in at least 3%, a conventional first mortgage covers the rest, and the state loan is repaid monthly at a fixed rate that the agency sets high enough to pay the bondholders back. Anyone who has lived in California for a year and earns no more than twice the area median income can apply, with no first-time-buyer requirement. The home must be new, the buyer must be its first owner, and its price cannot exceed 125% of the county's conforming loan limit, which works out to about $1.04 million in 41 counties and about $1.56 million in the ten most expensive ones in 2026. The Legislative Analyst's Office finds "no direct state or local costs," because borrowers' payments, not the General Fund, repay the bonds.
The Middle-Class Homeownership Loan under Proposition 37 is covering 17% of an $800,000 home so the buyer's own cash drops from $160,000 to $24,000. Prop 37, the "California Middle-Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the best-polling of them: 61% yes to 35% no in PPIC's September survey. No argument against it was filed, no opposition committee exists, and its Yes side reports $30.9 million from top donors, led by the state's Realtors, the carpenters' unions and the Brin-and-Doerr-funded Building a Better California. Governor Gavin Newsom, Xavier Becerra and the California Democratic Party support it, the California Republican Party is neutral, and the editorial boards split two to two. This explainer covers what the text does, who qualifies and at what price, how the loan compares with the help CalHFA already offers, the builder option, the consumer rules, the cost, the money, the argument and the polling.

The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds a chapter to the Health and Safety Code directing CalHFA to run a "Middle-Class Home Ownership Loan Program" and authorizing it to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds, the kind repaid by the program's own income rather than by the state. Each loan "shall finance no more than 17 percent of the purchase price" and must be secured by a second mortgage behind the buyer's primary loan. The agency has to launch the program within one year of the measure taking effect, and it decides how many bonds to sell and when, "in a manner that minimizes interest costs and encourages broad investor participation."
The repayment design is in section 51515.05. CalHFA sets the interest rates, amortization schedules and payment terms "on terms the agency determines practical and favorable to applicants and at levels necessary, to the greatest extent possible, to pay the principal, interest, and other amounts due with respect to the bonds," plus "all costs of administration." The loans must be fixed-rate, the agency may let a borrower use the loan for closing costs if that "balances the interests of borrowers and bond investors," and every bond must state on its face that it "shall not be deemed to constitute a debt or liability or a pledge of the faith and credit of the State of California." The Legislative Analyst's Office (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm) notes that CalHFA "also would be required to keep interest costs for homebuyers as low as possible," and that the measure leaves the rate itself to the agency.
The program is restricted to new homes. A "qualified new home" is a newly built house, townhome, row house, condominium or manufactured home, or a unit in a former nonresidential building converted to housing, in either case "where the borrower is the first purchaser." Builders may sell qualified homes to anyone; only buyers using the loan must meet the program's rules. California’s Proposition 37 would let buyers put 3% down on a new home, with a state loan covering the other 17%
Proposition 37 would let CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds and lend buyers of newly built homes up to 17% of the price, so they can put 3% down. The loan is a fixed-rate second mortgage with monthly payments. Here is who qualifies, the county price caps, the cost and who is behind it.
by
Pat Sharyon | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/pat/)
Updated
October 17, 2026

California's Proposition 37 is asking voters to let the state lend new-home buyers up to 17% of the purchase price
Proposition 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency borrow up to $25 billion from investors and lend it to buyers of newly built homes as a second mortgage covering up to 17% of the price. The buyer puts in at least 3%, a conventional first mortgage covers the rest, and the state loan is repaid monthly at a fixed rate that the agency sets high enough to pay the bondholders back. Anyone who has lived in California for a year and earns no more than twice the area median income can apply, with no first-time-buyer requirement. The home must be new, the buyer must be its first owner, and its price cannot exceed 125% of the county's conforming loan limit, which works out to about $1.04 million in 41 counties and about $1.56 million in the ten most expensive ones in 2026. The Legislative Analyst's Office finds "no direct state or local costs," because borrowers' payments, not the General Fund, repay the bonds.
The Middle-Class Homeownership Loan under Proposition 37 is covering 17% of an $800,000 home so the buyer's own cash drops from $160,000 to $24,000. Prop 37, the "California Middle-Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the best-polling of them: 61% yes to 35% no in PPIC's September survey. No argument against it was filed, no opposition committee exists, and its Yes side reports $30.9 million from top donors, led by the state's Realtors, the carpenters' unions and the Brin-and-Doerr-funded Building a Better California. Governor Gavin Newsom, Xavier Becerra and the California Democratic Party support it, the California Republican Party is neutral, and the editorial boards split two to two. This explainer covers what the text does, who qualifies and at what price, how the loan compares with the help CalHFA already offers, the builder option, the consumer rules, the cost, the money, the argument and the polling.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds a chapter to the Health and Safety Code directing CalHFA to run a "Middle-Class Home Ownership Loan Program" and authorizing it to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds, the kind repaid by the program's own income rather than by the state. Each loan "shall finance no more than 17 percent of the purchase price" and must be secured by a second mortgage behind the buyer's primary loan. The agency has to launch the program within one year of the measure taking effect, and it decides how many bonds to sell and when, "in a manner that minimizes interest costs and encourages broad investor participation."
The repayment design is in section 51515.05. CalHFA sets the interest rates, amortization schedules and payment terms "on terms the agency determines practical and favorable to applicants and at levels necessary, to the greatest extent possible, to pay the principal, interest, and other amounts due with respect to the bonds," plus "all costs of administration." The loans must be fixed-rate, the agency may let a borrower use the loan for closing costs if that "balances the interests of borrowers and bond investors," and every bond must state on its face that it "shall not be deemed to constitute a debt or liability or a pledge of the faith and credit of the State of California." The program is restricted to new homes. A "qualified new home" is a newly built house, townhome, row house, condominium or manufactured home, or a unit in a former nonresidential building converted to housing, in either case "where the borrower is the first purchaser." Builders may sell qualified homes to anyone; only buyers using the loan must meet the program's rules. relatively little new for-sale housing, particularly condominiums and townhomes, has
been built in recent years, and many existing assistance programs target lower-income
households rather than middle-income buyers.
Current Housing Assistance: The California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA),
established by the 1975 Housing and Home Finance Act, administers many programs to
assist people with low and moderate incomes in renting and buying homes. Since many
people can afford the mortgage payment but struggle with a down payment, some of
these programs may include "second mortgages” (loans that must be repaid) that serve
as down payment assistance. Existing law authorizes CalHFA to issue up to $13.15
billion in revenue bonds to meet these needs.
Builders have long argued that California’s existing right-to-repair and construction-
defect litigation framework makes developing for-sale multifamily housing and
condominiums financially risky, contributing to the limited construction of new condos
and townhomes in the state.
Construction Defects: Current law (Title 7 of the Civil Code, passed in 2002 as SB 800
Right to Repair Act) establishes detailed construction standards and requires
homeowners to complete a mandatory pre-litigation notice-and-repair process, allowing
builders to inspect and fix alleged defects before a lawsuit may be filed. It also defines
liability broadly for violations of those standards (even without resulting damage), sets
problem-specific timelines, and emphasizes repair as the primary remedy while
regulating how disputes must be resolved."InDepth" Summaries for November 2026 Propositions
League of Women Voters of California Education FundPage 29
Related Legislation: Voters are also considering a separate $10 billion general
obligation bond for affordable housing (SB 417) on the same ballot. Unlike the revenue
bonds in this initiative, general obligation bonds are repaid directly from the state’s
General Fund.
Proposed Proposition
This program is primarily aimed at households with moderate to higher incomes who
may not qualify for existing CalHFA programs but still struggle to afford home prices in
California.
Main Provisions – Second Mortgage Program: This measure authorizes CalHFA to
issue $25 billion in revenue bonds (separate from its existing bond authority) to fund the
"Middle-Class Homeownership Loan Program".
● Borrower Eligibility: Applicants must have been a California resident for at least
one year and earn no more than 200% of the Area Median Income (AMI) of the
county where the home is purchased.
● The Loan: Provides a secondary mortgage for up to 17% of the purchase price.
● Borrower Funds: The applicant must provide at least a 3% down payment from
their own personal funds (not a grant or other loan).
● Occupancy: The applicant must occupy the home as a primary residence within
60 days of closing.
● Property Eligibility: Limited to newly constructed homes, townhomes,
condominiums, or repurposed nonresidential units where the applicant is the first
purchaser.
● Sales Price and Loan Limit Cap: The sales price is capped at 125% of the
conforming loan limit (ranging from approx. $1M to $1.5M in 2025).
● Foreclosure Rights: The measure allows CalHFA to follow different foreclosure
procedures on these loans than those required for some private lenders.
Consumer Protections: The following consumer protections will be established:
● Lender Origination Fee: A lender may charge an origination fee of up to 0.5% or
$290, whichever is greater.
● Early Payment Penalty: No penalty can be charged for early payment of the
second mortgage.
● Fixed Rate Mortgage: The second mortgage shall be a fixed-rate mortgage."InDepth" Summaries for November 2026 Propositions
League of Women Voters of California Education FundPage 30
● Credit Score: If the applicant’s credit score falls below the program minimum, the
lender shall allow the applicant to submit financial records to enable “cash flow
underwriting” to qualify the applicant for more favorable terms under the program.
● Realtor/Broker: Applicant shall retain a licensed California real estate agent or
broker.
Main Provisions – Qualified Builder Option: Developers/builders can voluntarily “opt-
in” to a Qualified Builder program. These changes affect how disputes over construction
quality are handled and may change the balance of protections between homeowners
and builders. However, supporters and opponents may disagree on whether these
changes improve the efficiency of disputes or reduce homeowner protections.
● Builder Liability: Developer/Builder must accept full liability for all labor law
violations committed by any of their contractors or subcontractors at any tier,
including:
o Valid state contractor’s license
o Worker’s compensation insurance
o Labor law violations
o Employer obligations under Unemployment Insurance Code (Div 1 & 6)
● Modified Right to Repair: Participating developers and builders are subject to
modified "Right-to-Repair" procedures, including:
o The ability to communicate directly with homeowners during pre-litigation.
o Homeowners must provide more detailed notices that identify each
residence and the specific violation, and these notices must be signed by
each homeowner alleging a violation.
o The right to obtain a written release/waiver from the homeowner once
repairs are finished to the owner's satisfaction.
o A cap on attorney fees at 30% of total recovery.
o Builder may bring a motion to dismiss litigation if claimant has not taken
affirmative action within 120 days.
Initiator: Robert M. Hertzberg, former State Senate Majority Leader and Assembly
Speaker. Hertzberg represented the San Fernando Valley - 18th Senate District and
40th Assembly District."InDepth" Summaries for November 2026 Propositions
League of Women Voters of California Education FundPage 31
Related Legislation
California’s 2026 Housing Strategy: Funding and Reform
Proposition 1 - The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026
Proposition 37 - The California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home
Construction Act of 2026
Proposition 45 - The Building an Affordable California Act
The November 2026 ballot presents voters with a multi-layered approach to the state’s
housing shortage. While they share the goal of increasing housing availability, they
function as different "tools" in the toolkit: Props 1 and 37 provide financing for different
income levels. At the same time, Prop 45 seeks to reform the regulatory process to
ensure those projects are built faster.
1. The Funding Mechanisms: Prop 1 & Prop 37
These two bond measures are complementary, as they target different populations,
provide for different housing types, and use different financial structures:
Target Populations: Prop 1 focuses on providing a mix of subsidized rental housing and
homeownership assistance for families with low incomes, farm workers, students,
veterans, and individuals experiencing homelessness, to name a few. Prop 37 assists
moderate-income households (up to 200% of Area Median Income) who earn too much
to qualify for traditional assistance programs yet are still priced out of homeownership.
Project Scope: Prop 1 funds both construction of new housing (rental and permanent)
and the preservation and rehabilitation of existing affordable housing. Prop 37 is strictly
limited to newly constructed homes to incentivize an increase in total housing supply.
Financial Impact: Prop 1 uses General Obligation bonds, which are repaid by the state
and its taxpayers via the General Fund (though the veterans' portion is intended to be
repaid through their mortgage payments). Prop 37 uses Revenue bonds, which are
intended to be self-sustaining and repaid solely by the participating homeowners,
carrying no direct cost to the state budget.
2. Removing The Regulatory “Roadblock”: Prop 45
While Props 1 and 37 provide the “fuel” (funding), Prop 45 aims to “clear the road” by
addressing the environmental, permitting, and litigation delays that supporters claim
make housing too expensive to build. Prop 45 establishes strict, mandatory time limits
for environmental reviews (CEQA) and permit approvals (PSA) for “essential projects,”
which explicitly includes the housing types funded by Props 1 and 37. Prop 45 also"InDepth" Summaries for November 2026 Propositions
League of Women Voters of California Education FundPage 32
requires courts to resolve legal challenges to essential projects within mandatory time
limits to prevent years of construction delays.
Voter Perspective
While these measures could appear complementary (in the interest of expanding
access to more affordable housing in California), critics express concern that placing
several complex housing initiatives on a single ballot may cause voter confusion or
dilute support for individual measures.
Fiscal Analysis
The Legislative Analyst’s Office found no direct state or local costs as the program is
designed to be self-sustaining. The $25 billion in bond debt and all state administrative
expenses are intended to be repaid by participating homeowners through their
mortgage payments and interest. The LAO notes that the program's ultimate impact will
depend on investor demand, borrower participation, and whether the measure
increases home construction and homeownership.
Supporters Say
● Builds More Homes: By limiting assistance to newly built housing, supporters
argue the measure encourages additional home construction.
● Reduces Down-Payment Barriers: Helps households that can afford monthly
mortgage payments but struggle to save for a large down payment.
● Expands Access: Builds on current programs by helping middle-income
households who may not qualify for existing programs.
● No Taxpayer Risk: Uses revenue bonds repaid by homeowners, protecting the
state's General Fund.
● Consumer Protections: Includes borrower safeguards and financial protections
while expanding access to homeownership.
Opponents Say
No official ballot argument against Proposition 37 was submitted. The following
concerns have been raised in policy discussions regarding the measure:
● Default Exposure: With less upfront investment (3% down payment), borrowers
have a smaller financial stake, which may increase risk to lenders and
bondholders."InDepth" Summaries for November 2026 Propositions
League of Women Voters of California Education FundPage 33
● Location Risk: The measure does not prioritize existing urban areas, risking
more development in greenfield and agricultural areas, which leads to less
investment in existing communities, could increase travel distances and could
affect transportation and environmental conditions.
● Protection Limits: Modified right-to-repair rules and attorney fee caps may
make it harder for homeowners to hold builders accountable for poor
construction.
● Voter Confusion: Having multiple housing-related measures on the same ballot
may confuse voters and dilute support for other affordable housing efforts.
For More Information
Supporters:
● Yes on 37 - VoteYeson37.com
● Danny Curtin, Director, California Conference of Carpenters
● Fiona Ma, Board Member, California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA)
● David West, Chair, California State Commanders Veterans Council
Opponents:
● No official opposition campaign was identified in the Official Voter Information
Guide.
Spending in Support/Opposition
Cal Access - Prop 37:
Cal Access for Prop 37 Campaign Contributions
In Support as of 9/10/26 - $16.5M Total. Top 6 Contributors:
Building a Better California $6,000,000
Calif Assoc of Realtors Issues Mobilization PAC (IMPAC) 5,000,000
Homeownership for Families, Sponsored by Calif Assoc of Realtors 4,000,000
United Brotherhood of Carpenters & Joiners of America 750,000
Western States Regional Council of Carpenters Issues Committee 400,000
Northern California Carpenters Regional Council Issues PAC 400,000"InDepth" Summaries for November 2026 Propositions
League of Women Voters of California Education FundPage 34
Choosing Yes or No
A "YES" vote means: You support authorizing $25 billion in revenue bonds for a
middle-class second-mortgage program and allowing developers to access modified
construction-defect rules if they accept full liability for subcontractor labor violations.
PER THE VOTER INFORMATION GUIDE: The state would create a new homebuying
assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the
program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners’ payments on their home loans.
A "NO" vote means: You oppose this bond-funded loan program; existing CalHFA
homeownership assistance and state construction defect laws would remain
unchanged. PER THE VOTER INFORMATION GUIDE: The state would not be required
to create a new homebuying assistance program.

Proposition 38 – Bonds for Research on the Immune System
Initiative Statute
The Question
Should California authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds to fund immunology
and immunotherapy research, including approximately $4.2 billion for a single nonprofit
research institute affiliated with the University of California and $4.2 billion for grants to
other California public and nonprofit universities and research institutions?
The Situation
Medical Research Funding
Medical research and development (R&D) generally moves through several stages:
1. Basic research—often conducted by universities and nonprofit research
institutions—focuses on understanding disease and developing new scientific
knowledge.
2. Applied and clinical research then evaluates potential therapies in laboratory and
patient settings before treatments can be approved for public use.
According to the Legislative Analyst's Office, private industry provides approximately
65% of U.S. medical research and development funding, while the federal government
provides about 25%. State governments play a comparatively small role in funding
medical research. Federal agencies, including the National Institutes of Health (NIH),
have historically been major sources of funding for biomedical research. Federal
funding levels and research priorities can change over time, creating uncertainty for
long-term research projects. While funding medical research has traditionally been a
federal responsibility, there remains a question of whether state taxpayers should
assume a larger role.
Immunology and Immunotherapy
Immunology is the study of the body's immune system. Immunotherapy involves
treatments that use or modify the immune system to prevent, treat, or cure disease.
Although immunotherapy is most commonly associated with cancer treatment,
researchers are also investigating its potential use in Alzheimer's disease, heart
disease, autoimmune disorders, diabetes, infectious diseases, and other chronic
conditions. California is home to numerous immunology and immunotherapy research
programs, including those affiliated with UCLA, UCSF, UC San Diego, UC Irvine,
Stanford University, and other nonprofit research institutions."InDepth" Summaries for November 2026 Propositions
League of Women Voters of California Education FundPage 36
Previous State Research Bonds
California voters have previously approved large bond measures to support biomedical
research.
Proposition 71 (2004) authorized $3 billion in general obligation bonds and created the
California Institute for Regenerative Medicine (CIRM) to support stem cell research.
This measure passed 59% to 41%.
Proposition 14 (2020) authorized an additional $5.5 billion in general obligation bonds
to continue funding CIRM. This measure passed 51% to 49%.
Unlike Props 71 and 14, which distributed funding broadly through CIRM grant
programs, this measure directs 50% of its funding to a single qualifying institute.
Supporters of these measures cite the development of research facilities, clinical trials,
biotechnology companies, workforce training programs, and medical discoveries
associated with CIRM-funded research. Studies commissioned by supporters estimated
that CIRM funding contributed to thousands of jobs and billions of dollars of economic
activity in California.
Critics note that scientific advances often take decades to develop and that direct
financial returns to taxpayers through royalties and licensing revenue have been
relatively modest compared with the overall public investment. In fact, the LAO’s
analysis of Prop 14 reported that as of 2019, CIRM grant recipients had contributed
$352,560 in total invention-related income to the state. They also point to governance
and conflict-of-interest concerns that emerged during CIRM's operation.
Unlike CIRM, which distributes funding across many institutions through a grant
process, this measure would direct half of all bond proceeds to a single research
institute while distributing the remaining funds through competitive grants.
Proposed Proposition
The California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative would authorize $8.4 billion
in state general obligation bonds, issued incrementally as funding is requested, for
immunology and immunotherapy research. The state would repay the bonds, with
interest, from the General Fund over time."InDepth" Summaries for November 2026 Propositions
League of Women Voters of California Education FundPage 37
The measure allocates funds as follows:
Single Research Institute — 50% ($4.2 billion)
Half of all bond proceeds would be awarded to a single nonprofit medical research
institute selected by the California Department of Public Health. The institute must meet
detailed eligibility criteria, including:
● An affiliation agreement with a University of California campus
● Existence before January 1, 2025
● A specific focus on immunology and immunotherapy research
● Demonstrate significant philanthropic funding commitments
● Maintain vaccine-development and microbiome-research programs
● Control a large research facility site of specific square footage
● Include UC representatives in governance
● DPH may modify these criteria only if no institute meets the original requirements
and only to the “minimum amount of modification necessary”
The measure does not identify any institution by name, and it is unclear how many
institutions would satisfy all eligibility requirements. Some observers may note,
however, that the eligibility requirements appear similar to publicly described
characteristics of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy (CIII), a
nonprofit institute affiliated with UCLA that was established with substantial
philanthropic support, including funding from initiative proponent Gary K. Michelson.
Competitive Grants — 50% ($4.2 billion)
The remaining funds would be distributed through research grants to California-based
public and nonprofit universities and nonprofit research institutions. Grant funding would
support research projects in immunology and immunotherapy selected through a review
process overseen by a newly created Advisory and Accountability Research Council.
Additional Provisions:
Disease Focus: At least $4.2 billion of the total bond funding must support research
related to cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's disease. The measure also

California’s Proposition 37 would let buyers put 3% down on a new home, with a state loan covering the other 17%
Proposition 37 would let CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds and lend buyers of newly built homes up to 17% of the price, so they can put 3% down. The loan is a fixed-rate second mortgage with monthly payments. Here is who qualifies, the county price caps, the cost and who is behind it.

California's Proposition 37 is asking voters to let the state lend new-home buyers up to 17% of the purchase price
Proposition 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency borrow up to $25 billion from investors and lend it to buyers of newly built homes as a second mortgage covering up to 17% of the price. The buyer puts in at least 3%, a conventional first mortgage covers the rest, and the state loan is repaid monthly at a fixed rate that the agency sets high enough to pay the bondholders back. Anyone who has lived in California for a year and earns no more than twice the area median income can apply, with no first-time-buyer requirement. The home must be new, the buyer must be its first owner, and its price cannot exceed 125% of the county's conforming loan limit, which works out to about $1.04 million in 41 counties and about $1.56 million in the ten most expensive ones in 2026. The Legislative Analyst's Office finds "no direct state or local costs," because borrowers' payments, not the General Fund, repay the bonds.
The Middle-Class Homeownership Loan under Proposition 37 is covering 17% of an $800,000 home so the buyer's own cash drops from $160,000 to $24,000. Prop 37, the "California Middle-Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the best-polling of them: 61% yes to 35% no in PPIC's September survey. No argument against it was filed, no opposition committee exists, and its Yes side reports $30.9 million from top donors, led by the state's Realtors, the carpenters' unions and the Brin-and-Doerr-funded Building a Better California. Governor Gavin Newsom, Xavier Becerra and the California Democratic Party support it, the California Republican Party is neutral, and the editorial boards split two to two. This explainer covers what the text does, who qualifies and at what price, how the loan compares with the help CalHFA already offers, the builder option, the consumer rules, the cost, the money, the argument and the polling.

Each loan "shall finance no more than 17 percent of the purchase price" and must be secured by a second mortgage behind the buyer's primary loan. The agency has to launch the program within one year of the measure taking effect, and it decides how many bonds to sell and when, "in a manner that minimizes interest costs and encourages broad investor participation."
The repayment design is in section 51515.05. CalHFA sets the interest rates, amortization schedules and payment terms "on terms the agency determines practical and favorable to applicants and at levels necessary, to the greatest extent possible, to pay the principal, interest, and other amounts due with respect to the bonds," plus "all costs of administration." The loans must be fixed-rate, the agency may let a borrower use the loan for closing costs if that "balances the interests of borrowers and bond investors," and every bond must state on its face that it "shall not be deemed to constitute a debt or liability or a pledge of the faith and credit of the State of California." CalHFA may add minimum credit scores and debt-to-income limits to satisfy Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac or FHA standards, and it may set a longer residency requirement. The LAO's October 2025 letter (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0013A1%29.pdf) to the Attorney General makes the point the ballot summary leaves out: an applicant "would not need to be a first-time homebuyer."
The price cap is a formula rather than a dollar figure: 125% of the one-unit conforming loan limit the Federal Housing Finance Agency publishes for the county each year. The FHFA set the 2026 baseline at $832,750 (https://www.fhfa.gov/news/news-release/fhfa-announces-conforming-loan-limit-values-for-2026), up 3.26% from 2025, with a ceiling of $1,249,125 in the highest-cost areas. Applying the measure's formula to the FHFA's county table (https://www.fhfa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-11/FullCountyLoanLimitList2026_HERA-BASED_FINAL_FLAT.xlsx) gives a 2026 cap of $1,040,938 in the 41 counties at the baseline, from Sacramento and Fresno to Riverside and San Bernardino, and $1,561,406 in the ten counties at the ceiling: Los Angeles, Orange, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Santa Cruz and San Benito. Seven counties sit between, including San Diego at $1,380,000 and Ventura at $1,293,750. The income ceiling moves with local incomes in the same way. Using the Department of Housing and Community Development's 2026 State Income Limits (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/income-limits-2026.pdf) as an illustration, a family of four could earn up to $216,200 in Los Angeles County, $261,800 in San Diego County, $401,600 in San Francisco and $194,200 in Fresno or Kern and still qualify. The measure does not say which income table CalHFA must use, so those figures show the shape of the rule rather than the agency's eventual numbers.

Price caps are our calculation from the measure (125% of the county conforming loan limit in the FHFA's annual report). Forty-one counties sit at the 2026 baseline limit of $832,750, so their cap is $1,040,938; ten Bay Area and Southern California counties sit at the $1,249,125 ceiling, so their cap is $1,561,406. Income ceilings use HCD's 2026 State Income Limits as an illustration; the measure says CalHFA will apply "the area median income for a family of the same size in the county or metropolitan statistical area," adjusted for family size, and the agency has not yet said which income table it would use.
PPIC's Eric McGhee calculated (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/) in October that 91% of California renters would have met the income test in 2024, the most recent Census year, and that the price cap "would have covered a home sold for as much as $1.15 million in 2024," about 50% above that December's statewide median. Eligibility, he wrote, "is not purchasing power": at 7% mortgage rates and Fannie Mae's 36% debt-to-income ceiling, an entry-level new home was out of reach for 56% of renters even with the down payment solved.
California's existing down payment programs defer repayment while Prop 37's loan is repaid monthly:
CalHFA already runs down payment help, and the comparison explains most of the debate. Its MyHome Assistance Program (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/myhome.htm) is a "deferred-payment junior loan" of up to 3.5% of the price on an FHA loan or 3% on a conventional one, for first-time buyers within CalHFA's income limits, with nothing due until the home is sold, refinanced or paid off. Its Dream For All Shared Appreciation Loan (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/dream/index.htm) lends up to 20% of the price, capped at $150,000, to first-generation and first-time buyers, and is repaid with the original amount plus 20% of the home's appreciation (15% for buyers at or below 80% of area median income) when the home changes hands. Dream For All is funded by budget appropriations and rationed by lottery; the 2026 application portal closed on March 16 and vouchers went out in May. Proposition 1 on the same ballot would add $1.1 billion (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm) in general obligation bond money for homeownership programs of this deferred kind, aimed at low- and moderate-income first-time buyers.
Prop 37's loan is different in three ways. It is open to anyone under 200% of AMI, not only first-time buyers. It is repaid monthly, because the bonds behind it have to be serviced from borrowers' payments. And it is limited to new construction. The California Budget & Policy Center's analysis (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/will-proposition-37-make-homeownership-more-affordable-its-not-guaranteed/) puts the first two together: the silent-second structure of today's programs "ensures that the downpayment assistance doesn't compete with the first mortgage, groceries, utility bills, or other basic needs in a family's monthly budget," while Prop 37's second mortgage "could also likely carry higher interest rates above conventional first mortgage rates," because investors in bonds backed by second liens "may therefore require a higher return." The measure's hardship clause lets a borrower ask CalHFA to defer "monthly interest payments" temporarily, which the Budget Center reads as confirmation that monthly payments are the design.
Down payment help in California today vs Proposition 37:
Feature CalHFA MyHome Assistance (today) CalHFA Dream For All (today) Proposition 37 middle-class homeownership loan
Help with the down payment Up to 3.5% of the price (FHA) or 3% (conventional) Up to 20% of the price, capped at $150,000 Up to 17% of the price; buyer puts in at least 3% from their own funds
How it is repaid Deferred-payment junior loan: nothing due until the home is sold, refinanced or paid off Deferred: original amount plus 20% of the home's appreciation (15% for buyers at or below 80% of AMI) when the home is sold or the first mortgage is paid off A fixed-rate second mortgage with monthly payments sized to repay the bonds and CalHFA's costs; hardship deferral of interest only on request
Who qualifies First-time homebuyers within CalHFA income limits, paired with a CalHFA first mortgage First-time and first-generation homebuyers; CalHFA income limits; vouchers by random drawing Any buyer resident in California for a year, earning up to 200% of area median income, who occupies the home within 60 days; no first-time-buyer rule
Which homes Single-family homes, approved condominiums and manufactured homes, new or existing New or existing Newly built homes, or units converted from nonresidential buildings, where the buyer is the first purchaser; price capped at 125% of the county conforming loan limit
Where the money comes from CalHFA program funds State budget appropriations, distributed in limited rounds (the 2026 application portal closed March 16) Up to $25 billion in CalHFA revenue bonds sold to investors; no General Fund repayment
Builder rules None specific None specific Optional "qualified builder" track: labor standards from the 2025 infill-housing law in exchange for modified construction-defect procedures and a 30% cap on homeowner attorneys' contingency fees
The proponents' case for monthly repayment is the cost it replaces. Buyers who put down less than 20% usually pay private mortgage insurance until they build equity, and the McClatchy editorial board, which recommends (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317470188.html) a yes vote, wrote that proponents "have modeled relatively high second-mortgage rates and found buyers could still save money compared with private mortgage insurance." Nothing in the text guarantees a below-market rate; the argument in favor promises "below-market, fixed-rate loans," and the Orange County Register's editorial board wrote (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/20/endorsement-no-on-proposition-37-a-risky-25-billion-housing-experiment/) that the claim "rests on the assumption that foundations and non-profits will be willing to buy the bonds at a below-market interest rate of 3%," failing which CalHFA "will sell the bonds in the market and pay market interest rates."
Prop 37's qualified builder option trades labor standards for modified construction-defect rules:
Any developer can sell homes into the program. Section 51515.02 adds a voluntary "qualified builder option" for those who certify to CalHFA that their homes will meet the program's eligibility rules; the agency must confirm participation within 30 days, and the letter can be used to market and finance the project. A participating builder takes on the labor and enforcement provisions of Public Resources Code section 21080.66 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=21080.66), the 2025 infill-housing CEQA exemption, which require prevailing wages on fully affordable projects, apply the state's skilled-workforce standards to buildings over 85 feet, extend wage-theft liability under Labor Code section 218.8 to the developer, and let joint labor-management committees sue contractors on workers' behalf. The builder also becomes liable for its contractors' and subcontractors' unemployment-insurance, workers' compensation and licensing violations.
In exchange, homes built under the option get a modified version of the Right to Repair Act's pre-litigation process. A defect notice must identify each home and each alleged violation and be signed by each homeowner; the builder may communicate directly with homeowners during the process; the builder may obtain a written release for completed repairs, which current law, as the LAO's letter notes, does not allow; a builder may move to dismiss a stayed case if the homeowner has not acted within 120 days; and the builder must disclose the special rules in writing before escrow closes. For any qualified new home, built under the option or not, attorneys' contingency fees in a defect case are capped at 30% of the recovery unless a court approves more. The modified procedures fall away if a builder sells a home for more than 25% above the price cap, a point proponent Robert Hertzberg confirmed to the Register's board. The California Conference of Carpenters is a signer of the ballot argument and its affiliates have given $1.7 million to the campaign.
Proposition 37's second mortgages are exempt from a 2025 foreclosure-protection law and carry a 0.5% fee cap:
Section 51515.04 sets the consumer rules. CalHFA must limit lender fees, ban prepayment penalties and require fixed rates. A lender may charge an origination fee of no more than 0.5% or $290, whichever is greater, and no other fee without the agency's approval. An applicant whose credit score falls short may submit bank statements, pay stubs and rent history for "cashflow underwriting." Every applicant must retain a licensed California real estate agent or broker "to ensure that the home buyer receives adequate representation." CalHFA must require homeowner education where it would help and provide for an independent annual audit.
One clause runs the other way. Subdivision (g) states that Civil Code section 2924.13 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2924.13) "shall not apply to any middle-class home ownership loans made under this chapter." That section, added by AB 130 in June 2025, targets dormant second mortgages: it makes it an unlawful practice for a subordinate-mortgage servicer to go three years without writing to the borrower, to skip required transfer notices, or to foreclose on a debt it has reported as written off or after the statute of limitations has run, and it requires a recorded certification of compliance before any nonjudicial foreclosure. Prop 37 loans, which are subordinate mortgages serviced by CalHFA's contracted lenders, would sit outside those rules. The text does not say why.
The Legislative Analyst finds no direct state cost and three unknowns for Proposition 37:
The LAO's ballot analysis and its October 6, 2025 letter reach the same conclusion in nearly the same words: because the measure "uses the payments from homebuyers to repay bond investors, it would not result in direct state or local costs." The letter adds that the $25 billion "is in addition to the revenue bonds CalHFA already issues" for its other programs. Both documents then list what cannot be known yet: "the extent to which investors want to buy the bond," "how much the loans available under this proposed program cost homebuyers compared with other down payment assistance options," and "whether the program results in increased home construction and homebuying."
The Voter Information Guide's Overview of State Bond Debt (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm) does not count Prop 37 at all. It lists two General Fund-supported bonds on this ballot, Propositions 1 and 38, at about $1 billion a year combined, against the roughly $6 billion a year the state already pays on about $80 billion of outstanding bonds. The closest precedent for a self-repaying housing bond is in Prop 1 itself: its $1.25 billion veterans' home-loan bond is repaid by borrowers, and the LAO notes those payments "have always covered the amount owed on the bonds." The difference is that veterans' bonds are general obligation bonds the state stands behind if payments fall short; Prop 37's are revenue bonds that, by their own terms, it does not. The McClatchy board raised the political version of that risk: borrowers in trouble "will quickly discover that their second mortgage exists because California created and authorized this program," which "could create an expectation that the state bears some responsibility for protecting them."
Proposition 37's reach depends on interest rates and new construction, according to PPIC and the Budget Center:
The campaign says the measure "is expected to spur construction of roughly 190,000 new homes." California YIMBY, which took no position (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-37-2026/), worked the arithmetic the other way: $25 billion over 190,000 homes is about $130,000 of bond money per home, and the group argued "there is no shortage of buyers" for new ownership housing, so the subsidy would mostly raise prices unless it reached weaker markets. PPIC's McGhee estimated that if every loan went to a home at the maximum price with the full 17%, $25 billion would reach about 113,000 buyers; at the full 17% on entry-level homes, about 560,000, which he called "a reasonable central estimate." California would have needed 1.35 million more owner households in 2024 to match the rest of the country, and the 560,000 figure would close about 41% of that gap.
The homeownership gap is the proponents' starting point. The Census Bureau's state table (https://www.census.gov/housing/hvs/data/rates/tab3_state05_2026_hmr.xlsx) puts California's homeownership rate at 54.3% in the second quarter of 2026, the lowest of the 50 states except New York (52.4%), against a national rate (https://www.census.gov/housing/hvs/files/qtr226/Q226press.pdf) of 65.0%. The argument in favor says a 20% down payment on a median home "can require saving over $186,000"; the California Association of Realtors' latest report (https://www.car.org/en/aboutus/mediacenter/newsreleases/2026releases/august2026sales) put the median existing single-family price at $901,420 in August 2026, which makes 20% about $180,000 and 3% about $27,000. The Budget Center notes that the median California household held "just over $18,000" in checking and savings in 2025, so even 3% "could still almost or entirely clear out" what a typical family has, and that new homes more often carry HOA dues, Mello-Roos assessments and insurance problems in fire-prone areas.
Proposition 37's Yes side reports $30.9 million from Realtors, carpenters and Building a Better California with no opposition committee:
The Fair Political Practices Commission's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), updated October 14, shows $30.9 million in support of Prop 37 across two committees and no opposition committee large enough to appear. The main committee, "Yes on 37—California Homeownership," lists $23.9 million from its top contributors: $14.85 million from Homeownership for Families, a committee sponsored by the California Association of Realtors whose own top donors are the Realtors' Issues Mobilization PAC and the National Association of Realtors; $6 million from Building a Better California, the committee funded by Sergey Brin and John Doerr that is also the main opponent of the billionaire tax (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/); $1.25 million from the National Association of Realtors; $1.7 million from three carpenters' union committees; $50,000 from California Forever, the Solano County new-town developer; and $30,358 from the California Democratic Party. The Realtors' Homeownership for Families committee is listed separately with $7 million from the Realtors' PAC and the national association.
The Secretary of State's contribution tally (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-37-creates-loan-program-middle-income-buyers-qualified-new-homes-initiative-statute), which runs through October 6, shows $19.6 million for the Yes committee and "No committees identified" in opposition; the FPPC's later date accounts for the gap. The petition that qualified the measure was paid for by "CA Homes Committee," with major funding from Building a Better California, the California Association of Realtors and the United Brotherhood of Carpenters, according to the Secretary of State's Official Top Funders (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/top-funders/1990-top-funders-02-02-26.pdf) filing. The Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/initiatives/active-measures) lists Robert M. Hertzberg, the former Assembly Speaker and Senate majority leader, as proponent on A.G. File 25-0013A1, titled October 21, 2025. The Budget Center observes that because revenue bonds need no voter approval, the program "could have been enacted legislatively."
The argument for Proposition 37 promises zero taxpayer cost and no argument against was filed:
The argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by Danny Curtin of the California Conference of Carpenters, Treasurer Fiona Ma as a CalHFA board member and David West of the California State Commanders Veterans Council, says the measure "creates affordable homeownership opportunities for working and middle-class Californians and encourages new home construction—with ZERO COST TO TAXPAYERS." Nothing in the text guarantees a below-market rate; the argument in favor promises "below-market, fixed-rate loans," and the Orange County Register's editorial board wrote (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/20/endorsement-no-on-proposition-37-a-risky-25-billion-housing-experiment/) that the claim "rests on the assumption that foundations and non-profits will be willing to buy the bonds at a below-market interest rate of 3%," failing which CalHFA "will sell the bonds in the market and pay market interest rates."
Prop 37's qualified builder option trades labor standards for modified construction-defect rules:
Any developer can sell homes into the program. Section 51515.02 adds a voluntary "qualified builder option" for those who certify to CalHFA that their homes will meet the program's eligibility rules; the agency must confirm participation within 30 days, and the letter can be used to market and finance the project. A participating builder takes on the labor and enforcement provisions of Public Resources Code section 21080.66 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=21080.66), the 2025 infill-housing CEQA exemption, which require prevailing wages on fully affordable projects, apply the state's skilled-workforce standards to buildings over 85 feet, extend wage-theft liability under Labor Code section 218.8 to the developer, and let joint labor-management committees sue contractors on workers' behalf. A defect notice must identify each home and each alleged violation and be signed by each homeowner; the builder may communicate directly with homeowners during the process; the builder may obtain a written release for completed repairs, which current law, as the LAO's letter notes, does not allow; a builder may move to dismiss a stayed case if the homeowner has not acted within 120 days; and the builder must disclose the special rules in writing before escrow closes. For any qualified new home, built under the option or not, attorneys' contingency fees in a defect case are capped at 30% of the recovery unless a court approves more. The modified procedures fall away if a builder sells a home for more than 25% above the price cap, a point proponent Robert Hertzberg confirmed to the Register's board. The California Conference of Carpenters is a signer of the ballot argument and its affiliates have given $1.7 million to the campaign.
Proposition 37's second mortgages are exempt from a 2025 foreclosure-protection law and carry a 0.5% fee cap:
Section 51515.04 sets the consumer rules. CalHFA must limit lender fees, ban prepayment penalties and require fixed rates. A lender may charge an origination fee of no more than 0.5% or $290, whichever is greater, and no other fee without the agency's approval. An applicant whose credit score falls short may submit bank statements, pay stubs and rent history for "cashflow underwriting." Every applicant must retain a licensed California real estate agent or broker "to ensure that the home buyer receives adequate representation." CalHFA must require homeowner education where it would help and provide for an independent annual audit.
One clause runs the other way. Subdivision (g) states that Civil Code section 2924.13 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2924.13) "shall not apply to any middle-class home ownership loans made under this chapter." That section, added by AB 130 in June 2025, targets dormant second mortgages: it makes it an unlawful practice for a subordinate-mortgage servicer to go three years without writing to the borrower, to skip required transfer notices, or to foreclose on a debt it has reported as written off or after the statute of limitations has run, and it requires a recorded certification of compliance before any nonjudicial foreclosure. Prop 37 loans, which are subordinate mortgages serviced by CalHFA's contracted lenders, would sit outside those rules. The text does not say why.
The Legislative Analyst finds no direct state cost and three unknowns for Proposition 37:
The LAO's ballot analysis and its October 6, 2025 letter reach the same conclusion in nearly the same words: because the measure "uses the payments from homebuyers to repay bond investors, it would not result in direct state or local costs." The letter adds that the $25 billion "is in addition to the revenue bonds CalHFA already issues" for its other programs. Both documents then list what cannot be known yet: "the extent to which investors want to buy the bond," "how much the loans available under this proposed program cost homebuyers compared with other down payment assistance options," and "whether the program results in increased home construction and homebuying."
The Voter Information Guide's Overview of State Bond Debt (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm) does not count Prop 37 at all. It lists two General Fund-supported bonds on this ballot, Propositions 1 and 38, at about $1 billion a year combined, against the roughly $6 billion a year the state already pays on about $80 billion of outstanding bonds. The closest precedent for a self-repaying housing bond is in Prop 1 itself: its $1.25 billion veterans' home-loan bond is repaid by borrowers, and the LAO notes those payments "have always covered the amount owed on the bonds." The difference is that veterans' bonds are general obligation bonds the state stands behind if payments fall short; Prop 37's are revenue bonds that, by their own terms, it does not. The McClatchy board raised the political version of that risk: borrowers in trouble "will quickly discover that their second mortgage exists because California created and authorized this program," which "could create an expectation that the state bears some responsibility for protecting them."
Proposition 37's reach depends on interest rates and new construction, according to PPIC and the Budget Center:
The campaign says the measure "is expected to spur construction of roughly 190,000 new homes." California YIMBY, which took no position (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-37-2026/), worked the arithmetic the other way: $25 billion over 190,000 homes is about $130,000 of bond money per home, and the group argued "there is no shortage of buyers" for new ownership housing, so the subsidy would mostly raise prices unless it reached weaker markets. PPIC's McGhee estimated that if every loan went to a home at the maximum price with the full 17%, $25 billion would reach about 113,000 buyers; at the full 17% on entry-level homes, about 560,000, which he called "a reasonable central estimate." California would have needed 1.35 million more owner households in 2024 to match the rest of the country, and the 560,000 figure would close about 41% of that gap.
The homeownership gap is the proponents' starting point. The Census Bureau's state table (https://www.census.gov/housing/hvs/data/rates/tab3_state05_2026_hmr.xlsx) puts California's homeownership rate at 54.3% in the second quarter of 2026, the lowest of the 50 states except New York (52.4%), against a national rate (https://www.census.gov/housing/hvs/files/qtr226/Q226press.pdf) of 65.0%. The argument in favor says a 20% down payment on a median home "can require saving over $186,000"; the California Association of Realtors' latest report (https://www.car.org/en/aboutus/mediacenter/newsreleases/2026releases/august2026sales) put the median existing single-family price at $901,420 in August 2026, which makes 20% about $180,000 and 3% about $27,000. The Budget Center notes that the median California household held "just over $18,000" in checking and savings in 2025, so even 3% "could still almost or entirely clear out" what a typical family has, and that new homes more often carry HOA dues, Mello-Roos assessments and insurance problems in fire-prone areas.
Proposition 37's Yes side reports $30.9 million from Realtors, carpenters and Building a Better California with no opposition committee:
The Fair Political Practices Commission's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), updated October 14, shows $30.9 million in support of Prop 37 across two committees and no opposition committee large enough to appear. The Realtors' Homeownership for Families committee is listed separately with $7 million from the Realtors' PAC and the national association.
The Secretary of State's contribution tally (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-37-creates-loan-program-middle-income-buyers-qualified-new-homes-initiative-statute), which runs through October 6, shows $19.6 million for the Yes committee and "No committees identified" in opposition; the FPPC's later date accounts for the gap. File 25-0013A1, titled October 21, 2025. The Budget Center observes that because revenue bonds need no voter approval, the program "could have been enacted legislatively."

- No direct cost to taxpayers (revenue bonds, non-recourse to state)

- Targets new construction → supply-side effect
- Broad support: Newsom, unions, realtors, carpenters, mayors

CalHFA may add minimum credit scores and debt-to-income limits to satisfy Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac or FHA standards, and it may set a longer residency requirement. The LAO's October 2025 letter (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0013A1%29.pdf) to the Attorney General makes the point the ballot summary leaves out: an applicant "would not need to be a first-time homebuyer."
The price cap is a formula rather than a dollar figure: 125% of the one-unit conforming loan limit the Federal Housing Finance Agency publishes for the county each year. The FHFA set the 2026 baseline at $832,750 (https://www.fhfa.gov/news/news-release/fhfa-announces-conforming-loan-limit-values-for-2026), up 3.26% from 2025, with a ceiling of $1,249,125 in the highest-cost areas. Applying the measure's formula to the FHFA's county table (https://www.fhfa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-11/FullCountyLoanLimitList2026_HERA-BASED_FINAL_FLAT.xlsx) gives a 2026 cap of $1,040,938 in the 41 counties at the baseline, from Sacramento and Fresno to Riverside and San Bernardino, and $1,561,406 in the ten counties at the ceiling: Los Angeles, Orange, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Santa Cruz and San Benito. Seven counties sit between, including San Diego at $1,380,000 and Ventura at $1,293,750. The income ceiling moves with local incomes in the same way. Using the Department of Housing and Community Development's 2026 State Income Limits (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/income-limits-2026.pdf) as an illustration, a family of four could earn up to $216,200 in Los Angeles County, $261,800 in San Diego County, $401,600 in San Francisco and $194,200 in Fresno or Kern and still qualify. The measure does not say which income table CalHFA must use, so those figures show the shape of the rule rather than the agency's eventual numbers.
Proposition 37's 2026 price caps and income ceilings in 12 California counties:
