I now have the full text details confirmed:
- 30% attorney contingency fee cap applies to any action related to a "qualified new home" (not just qualified-builder homes)
- Civil Code 2924.13 foreclosure protections don't apply
- Rules exempt from APA
- Amendment requires >60% of each house
- Mandatory retention of a licensed real estate agent/broker
- No first-time buyer requirement
- Not "public works" — so no prevailing wage by default
- Bond cap $25B, non-recourse

Now let me weigh the decision.

Key considerations for the "better" vote:

Arguments for YES:
1. No direct taxpayer cost — revenue bonds, non-recourse, explicitly not a pledge of state faith and credit. LAO: "No direct state or local costs."
2. Asymmetric risk to the state: if the program flops, the state isn't on the hook (Chris Hoene of California Budget & Policy Center: "It could still work, and if it doesn't work, the state's not really on the hook").
3. Addresses a real barrier (down payment) for a large group; could reach ~560,000 buyers per PPIC's central estimate (41% of the ownership gap).
4. Targets new construction — designed to add supply rather than just bid up existing homes. Also addresses condo construction freeze via defect reform.
5. Broad, ideologically diverse support: Gov. Newsom, Xavier Becerra, California Democratic Party, labor unions (carpenters, nurses), veterans groups, chambers, builders, realtors, SPUR, SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee/McClatchy, Grow SF; even SD Taxpayers supports it.
6. Consumer protections in the text: fixed rate, no prepayment penalty, fee caps, cash-flow underwriting, mandatory buyer representation, homeowner education, annual independent audit.
7. Labor standards for participating builders (prevailing wage/skilled workforce/wage-theft liability) — unions support.
8. Polling: 65% yes / 32% no — strongest of all 14 measures; it will almost certainly pass, so a "no" vote is largely symbolic.

Arguments for NO:
1. The central economic flaw: it's a demand subsidy with no guarantee of rates. Second-lien revenue bonds are risky; investors will demand rates above first-mortgage rates (currently >7%). Adding a second mortgage of 17% at ~7-9% adds ~$900-1,000+/month on an $800k home — which is exactly the barrier most Californians can't overcome. PPIC: only ~40% of eligible renters could afford entry-level new home even with down payment solved; less than 0.5% could afford top-price homes. So the program may help relatively few, and mostly higher-income buyers.
2. Poor targeting: 200% AMI cap means families earning $400k+ in SF qualify; price caps up to $1.56M; no first-time-buyer requirement; no shared appreciation to recapture subsidy. So the subsidy flows disproportionately to white/Asian, higher-income households — the opposite of what's needed for the ownership gap. LWVC, Budget Center, SPUR cons all note this.
3. Price effects: In a supply-constrained market, demand subsidies get capitalized into prices. CA YIMBY: "there is no shortage of buyers for newly built ownership housing" → subsidy mostly raises prices of new homes, benefiting builders/sellers. AEI's Pinto: the same critique. That means the biggest winners are builders and realtors — who are precisely the funders ($33.6M, with CAR $18.7M and NAR $4.5M; plus Brin/Doerr's $6M and California Forever's $50k). And the text mandates that every borrower retain a licensed real estate agent — a guaranteed commission for the main funder. That's a self-interested giveaway.
4. It weakens homeowner legal protections: 30% cap on contingency fees for ALL qualified new homes; builders who opt in can obtain a release/waiver in exchange for repairs (currently prohibited by Civil Code 926); can move to dismiss after 120 days of homeowner inaction; and Prop 37 loans are exempt from Civil Code 2924.13's 2025 foreclosure protections for dormant second liens. Combined with rules exempt from APA and a >60% legislative vote to amend, these are durable, hard-to-reverse reductions in consumer rights enacted by initiative — and they weren't in the ballot title/summary or the argument in favor, which is a disclosure problem.
5. Leverage risk to households: 3% own cash + 17% second mortgage + 80% first mortgage = 100% LTV at purchase, monthly payments on both, plus HOA dues (70% of new homes), Mello-Roos assessments, and California's broken insurance market. In a downturn, these borrowers are deeply underwater quickly, and foreclosure on a second lien is where losses concentrate. HJTA: mass foreclosures risk. Even if the state isn't legally liable, political pressure for a bailout is real (McClatchy board raised it; Hoover flags moral-obligation risk).
6. It's not necessary via initiative: revenue bonds don't require voter approval — the legislature or CalHFA could do this, with proper targeting and consumer protections and without embedding defect-law changes. Budget Center notes this.
7. Editorial boards: Bay Area News Group (Mercury News/East Bay Times), OC Register, Press-Enterprise, San Diego Union-Tribune all say NO; SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee, SF Bay Guardian say YES. Split roughly evenly among major boards, but the "no" case is well-argued and comes from both left (LWVC, Budget Center) and right (HJTA, DeMaio).

Hmm. This is a genuinely close call. Let me think about the decisive factors.

The "no direct cost to taxpayers" argument is real and is the strongest point for yes. The state's downside is genuinely limited legally. If the bonds don't sell, nothing happens. If borrowers default, bondholders lose. So a "yes" is a low-risk-to-the-public experiment.

But that framing understates the actual harms:
(a) The harm falls on participating homebuyers — mostly moderate/upper-middle-income households taking on 100% financing at high rates. That's a real consumer-protection risk, and the measure strips protections (2924.13 exemption) while imposing a mandatory realtor.
(b) The construction-defect and attorney-fee changes reduce protections for ALL buyers of qualified new homes — not just program participants — and they're nearly permanent (>60% vote to amend). That's a substantive, durable weakening of consumer rights, buried in a housing-affordability measure, and it's the classic "logroll" that makes initiatives bad law. The LAO's own analysis describes it euphemistically as "more flexibility to developers."
(c) The economic evidence strongly suggests that in a supply-constrained market, demand subsidies get capitalized into prices. CA YIMBY — the state's leading pro-housing group — declined to support it, saying it would probably not make homeownership more affordable and would mostly benefit greenfield subdivisions. PPIC found affordability, not down payment, is the binding constraint for most. AEI's housing center concurs.
(d) It directs a huge subsidy at households earning up to $400k in high-cost counties, with price caps to $1.56M, no first-time-buyer priority, and no equity recapture — i.e., poor targeting relative to need, likely widening racial wealth gaps.
(e) It's funded overwhelmingly by realtors and developers who directly profit: CAR/NAR ~$23M of ~$34M. And the measure guarantees them a commission by requiring every borrower to retain a realtor. When the beneficiaries write the law and write the check, and the ballot summary doesn't mention the tort changes or the realtor mandate, that's a strong reason for skepticism.
(f) The premise of "below-market rates" depends on philanthropists buying taxable, non-recourse second-lien bonds at ~3%. That's speculative — Hertzberg won't name any. If it fails, rates will be above first-mortgage rates, and the program either does nothing or makes buyers worse off.

On the other hand: if it does nothing, the cost is near zero. That's a genuine point. But it's not zero: it does consume CalHFA administrative capacity, and if it works as designed at market rates, it increases household leverage and prices for new homes. Also, the tort-law changes take effect regardless of whether the bonds ever sell — the construction defect modifications and 30% fee cap apply to "qualified new homes" and "qualified builders" independent of bond issuance. That's a real, immediate, permanent policy change with zero offsetting benefit if the financing never materializes. That asymmetry is important: the costs (weakened homeowner legal rights, sprawl incentive) are certain-ish and permanent; the benefits are speculative.

Also worth noting: this could have been done legislatively with proper design (targeted to first-time/first-generation buyers, deferred-payment structure like Dream For All, shared appreciation to recapture public subsidy, infill priority). California already runs successful down-payment programs. Prop 37 is a worse-designed, less-targeted, harder-to-amend version.

Weighing: The decisive factors for me are (1) the poorly targeted subsidy to upper-income buyers of expensive homes funded by realtors who are guaranteed commissions; (2) the likely capitalization into higher new-home prices rather than improved affordability (CA YIMBY, PPIC, AEI all skeptical); (3) the permanent, buried weakening of homeowner construction-defect rights and foreclosure protections that applies regardless of whether the financing works; and (4) the risk of over-leveraging households into 100% financing at high rates with HOA/Mello-Roos/insurance costs on top.

Against that, the "no taxpayer cost" point is real but doesn't outweigh these — especially since the measure's legal protections for homeowners are reduced and its amendment threshold is >60%, making it hard to fix.

Hmm, but let me consider a counterweight: the "no cost, option value" argument is quite strong in expected-value terms. If there's, say, a 30% chance the program works well and helps hundreds of thousands of families buy homes and spurs construction, and a 70% chance it does little, and the state's fiscal downside is zero... wouldn't yes be the rational bet? 

But the costs aren't zero — they're borne by borrowers (over-leverage, higher monthly payments), by homeowners generally (weakened defect remedies, capped attorney fees — permanent), by excluded buyers (higher new-home prices), and by communities (sprawl). And the certain, permanent tort-law change is a real negative that occurs even in the "nothing happens" scenario. Also, the "state not on the hook" claim is legally true but politically fragile (moral obligation).

Also note the initiative is a statute amendable by >60% — with Democrats holding supermajorities in both houses, the legislature could actually amend it if needed (they have >60%). So the "hard to fix" argument is somewhat weaker in California's current political environment, though the amendment must be "consistent with and further the purposes" of the act, which constrains repeal of the tort provisions (arguably those further "building more middle-class housing"). Still, the legislature can't easily undo it.

Let me consider who the most credible analysts are:
- LAO: neutral, no direct costs, three big unknowns.
- PPIC (McGhee): could meaningfully help if targeted to lower-priced homes; but affordability is the binding constraint for most.
- CA YIMBY: neutral — "If we are going to subsidize demand for homes, this is one of the better ways to do it. However, given the ongoing shortage, such subsidies are unlikely to reduce costs."
- CA Budget & Policy Center: skeptical — "It's not guaranteed"; monthly repayment erodes benefit; equity concerns; sprawl; could have been done legislatively.
- LWVC: NO.
- HJTA: NO.
- Hoover: balanced, flags risks.
- SPUR: YES.
- Editorial boards: split. SF Chronicle YES; Sac Bee YES; Bay Area News Group NO; SDUT NO; OC Register NO; Press-Enterprise NO.

So among organizations with actual policy analysis (rather than interest), the left-of-center housing/budget experts are skeptical-to-opposed, the YIMBYs are neutral, and the pro-housing urbanist group SPUR supports. Interest groups (realtors, builders, carpenters) support.

Given the target of the question — "is it better to vote yes or no" — I should form a judgment. I lean NO, for these decisive reasons:

1. The benefit is speculative while the costs are concrete. The program's value depends entirely on investors buying taxable, non-recourse second-lien bonds at below-market rates — which no one has committed to. If rates are market-level (>7%), the second mortgage adds ~$900–$1,000+/month, which defeats the purpose for most households (PPIC: fewer than 40% of eligible renters could afford even an entry-level new home with the down payment solved).

2. Even in the best case, it mostly subsidizes higher-income buyers. 200% AMI = up to ~$400k for a family of four in SF/Santa Clara, on homes up to $1.56M, with no first-time-buyer requirement and no shared-appreciation recapture. Existing CalHFA programs (MyHome, Dream For All) are better targeted and use deferred/silent seconds that don't compete with the monthly budget. Prop 37 is a step backward in design.

3. In a supply-constrained market, demand subsidies get capitalized into prices — CA YIMBY, AEI, and standard economics agree. The likely winners are builders and realtors, who wrote and funded the measure ($33.6M, ~70% from CAR/NAR) and who secured a provision requiring every borrower to retain a licensed real estate agent — a guaranteed commission.

4. It permanently weakens homeowner legal protections in ways the ballot title, summary, and pro argument never mention: a 30% cap on contingency fees for construction-defect cases on any qualified new home; allowing builders to obtain releases in exchange for repairs (which Civil Code §926 currently prohibits); a dismissal motion if homeowners don't act within 120 days; and exemption of these second liens from Civil Code §2924.13's 2025 foreclosure protections. Plus program rules are exempt from the APA. These changes take effect whether or not a single bond is ever sold.

5. It loads households with 100% financing (3% cash + 17% second + 80% first) plus HOA dues (~70% of new homes), Mello-Roos assessments, and California's dysfunctional insurance market — the classic setup for underwater borrowers and second-lien losses in a downturn, with predictable political pressure for a state backstop despite the non-recourse language.

6. There's no reason to do this by initiative: revenue bonds don't need voter approval. The legislature or CalHFA could create a properly targeted version — first-time/first-generation buyers, deferred-payment structure, infill priority, no tort giveaways — without permanently embedding it in a statute amendable only by a 60% vote.

Counterweight acknowledged: no General Fund cost, real consumer protections on loan terms, new-construction targeting, and strong broad support. But on balance, the "no" case is stronger.

Hmm, let me double-check one thing: is the 30% contingency fee cap applicable to all "qualified new homes" or only those built by qualified builders? Reading the text: Section 51515.04(e)(2): "Notwithstanding any other law, in any action brought by a homeowner or group of homeowners asserting claims subject to the procedures set forth in Chapter 4 ... and Chapter 5 ... of Title 7 ... of the Civil Code or the procedures set forth in subparagraph (B) of paragraph (1) of this subdivision related to a qualified new home, the maximum allowable attorney contingency fee shall not exceed 30 percent..." — yes, it applies to any qualified new home, whether or not built under the qualified builder option. And (e)(1)(A) says Title 7 applies to qualified new homes except as modified in (B) for qualified-builder homes. So the fee cap is broader. Confirmed. Note that 30% is not an unusual contingency cap (it's roughly standard for the pre-litigation stage), but it does apply regardless of complexity, subject to court approval for more. It's a moderate change, not draconian. Still, it's a tort-reform provision bundled in.

Also, the release/waiver provision (e)(1)(B)(iii) is limited to qualified-builder homes, and it requires the homeowner be satisfied, release be knowing and voluntary, and not extend to unaddressed defects. That's actually fairly protective in drafting — more so than the critics suggest. Hmm. That tempers my concern #4 somewhat. The LAO's letter notes current law prohibits builders from obtaining a release in exchange for repair work; Prop 37 allows it, but with conditions. That's a genuine reduction in homeowner leverage (a homeowner who accepts repairs signs away claims about those defects) but it's bounded.

Still, the 2924.13 exemption is unexplained and cuts against consumers, and the APA exemption reduces transparency.

Let me also weigh: how much does one vote matter? It's polling 65-32, so it'll pass regardless. The question asks which is "better," so I should give my honest substantive judgment.

Let me do one more check: are there any reputable analyses suggesting the program would actually deliver below-market rates, e.g., has CalHFA or the campaign identified institutional investors? And is there anything about the requirement that the bonds qualify for CRA credit? Also let me verify the Sacramento Bee's YES reasoning and the SF Chronicle's YES reasoning, to steelman.

Actually, let me check one more important thing: whether there's any risk to CalHFA's existing programs or the state's credit rating, and whether CalHFA's board officially supports it. Also check the "Building a Better California" involvement (Brin/Doerr — they also fund No on 40 billionaire tax), which suggests a political trade. And California Forever's $50k (Solano new town developer — benefits from greenfield demand subsidy). These support the "interest-driven" critique.

I think I have enough. Let me do one final check on the pro-side steelman (SF Chronicle / Sac Bee editorials) to make sure I'm not missing a compelling argument.

CA YIMBY: "there is no shortage of buyers for newly built ownership housing" → subsidy mostly raises prices of new homes, benefiting builders/sellers. AEI's Pinto: the same critique. That means the biggest winners are builders and realtors — who are precisely the funders ($33.6M, with CAR $18.7M and NAR $4.5M; plus Brin/Doerr's $6M and California Forever's $50k). And the text mandates that every borrower retain a licensed real estate agent — a guaranteed commission for the main funder. That's a self-interested giveaway.
4. It weakens homeowner legal protections: 30% cap on contingency fees for ALL qualified new homes; builders who opt in can obtain a release/waiver in exchange for repairs (currently prohibited by Civil Code 926); can move to dismiss after 120 days of homeowner inaction; and Prop 37 loans are exempt from Civil Code 2924.13's 2025 foreclosure protections for dormant second liens. Combined with rules exempt from APA and a >60% legislative vote to amend, these are durable, hard-to-reverse reductions in consumer rights enacted by initiative — and they weren't in the ballot title/summary or the argument in favor, which is a disclosure problem.
5. Leverage risk to households: 3% own cash + 17% second mortgage + 80% first mortgage = 100% LTV at purchase, monthly payments on both, plus HOA dues (70% of new homes), Mello-Roos assessments, and California's broken insurance market. In a downturn, these borrowers are deeply underwater quickly, and foreclosure on a second lien is where losses concentrate. HJTA: mass foreclosures risk. Even if the state isn't legally liable, political pressure for a bailout is real (McClatchy board raised it; Hoover flags moral-obligation risk).
6. It's not necessary via initiative: revenue bonds don't require voter approval — the legislature or CalHFA could do this, with proper targeting and consumer protections and without embedding defect-law changes. Budget Center notes this.
7. Editorial boards: Bay Area News Group (Mercury News/East Bay Times), OC Register, Press-Enterprise, San Diego Union-Tribune all say NO; SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee, SF Bay Guardian say YES. Split roughly evenly among major boards, but the "no" case is well-argued and comes from both left (LWVC, Budget Center) and right (HJTA, DeMaio).

Hmm. This is a genuinely close call. Let me think about the decisive factors.

The "no direct cost to taxpayers" argument is real and is the strongest point for yes. The state's downside is genuinely limited legally. If the bonds don't sell, nothing happens. If borrowers default, bondholders lose. So a "yes" is a low-risk-to-the-public experiment.

But that framing understates the actual harms:
(a) The harm falls on participating homebuyers — mostly moderate/upper-middle-income households taking on 100% financing at high rates. That's a real consumer-protection risk, and the measure strips protections (2924.13 exemption) while imposing a mandatory realtor.
(b) The construction-defect and attorney-fee changes reduce protections for ALL buyers of qualified new homes — not just program participants — and they're nearly permanent (>60% vote to amend). That's a substantive, durable weakening of consumer rights, buried in a housing-affordability measure, and it's the classic "logroll" that makes initiatives bad law. The LAO's own analysis describes it euphemistically as "more flexibility to developers."
(c) The economic evidence strongly suggests that in a supply-constrained market, demand subsidies get capitalized into prices. CA YIMBY — the state's leading pro-housing group — declined to support it, saying it would probably not make homeownership more affordable and would mostly benefit greenfield subdivisions. PPIC found affordability, not down payment, is the binding constraint for most. AEI's housing center concurs.
(d) It directs a huge subsidy at households earning up to $400k in high-cost counties, with price caps to $1.56M, no first-time-buyer priority, and no equity recapture — i.e., poor targeting relative to need, likely widening racial wealth gaps.
(e) It's funded overwhelmingly by realtors and developers who directly profit: CAR/NAR ~$23M of ~$34M. And the measure guarantees them a commission by requiring every borrower to retain a realtor. When the beneficiaries write the law and write the check, and the ballot summary doesn't mention the tort changes or the realtor mandate, that's a strong reason for skepticism.
(f) The premise of "below-market rates" depends on philanthropists buying taxable, non-recourse second-lien bonds at ~3%. That's speculative — Hertzberg won't name any. If it fails, rates will be above first-mortgage rates, and the program either does nothing or makes buyers worse off.

On the other hand: if it does nothing, the cost is near zero. That's a genuine point. But it's not zero: it does consume CalHFA administrative capacity, and if it works as designed at market rates, it increases household leverage and prices for new homes. Also, the tort-law changes take effect regardless of whether the bonds ever sell — the construction defect modifications and 30% fee cap apply to "qualified new homes" and "qualified builders" independent of bond issuance. That's a real, immediate, permanent policy change with zero offsetting benefit if the financing never materializes. That asymmetry is important: the costs (weakened homeowner legal rights, sprawl incentive) are certain-ish and permanent; the benefits are speculative.

Also worth noting: this could have been done legislatively with proper design (targeted to first-time/first-generation buyers, deferred-payment structure like Dream For All, shared appreciation to recapture public subsidy, infill priority). California already runs successful down-payment programs. Prop 37 is a worse-designed, less-targeted, harder-to-amend version.

Weighing: The decisive factors for me are (1) the poorly targeted subsidy to upper-income buyers of expensive homes funded by realtors who are guaranteed commissions; (2) the likely capitalization into higher new-home prices rather than improved affordability (CA YIMBY, PPIC, AEI all skeptical); (3) the permanent, buried weakening of homeowner construction-defect rights and foreclosure protections that applies regardless of whether the financing works; and (4) the risk of over-leveraging households into 100% financing at high rates with HOA/Mello-Roos/insurance costs on top.

Against that, the "no taxpayer cost" point is real but doesn't outweigh these — especially since the measure's legal protections for homeowners are reduced and its amendment threshold is >60%, making it hard to fix.

Hmm, but let me consider a counterweight: the "no cost, option value" argument is quite strong in expected-value terms. If there's, say, a 30% chance the program works well and helps hundreds of thousands of families buy homes and spurs construction, and a 70% chance it does little, and the state's fiscal downside is zero... wouldn't yes be the rational bet? 

But the costs aren't zero — they're borne by borrowers (over-leverage, higher monthly payments), by homeowners generally (weakened defect remedies, capped attorney fees — permanent), by excluded buyers (higher new-home prices), and by communities (sprawl). And the certain, permanent tort-law change is a real negative that occurs even in the "nothing happens" scenario. Also, the "state not on the hook" claim is legally true but politically fragile (moral obligation).

Also note the initiative is a statute amendable by >60% — with Democrats holding supermajorities in both houses, the legislature could actually amend it if needed (they have >60%). So the "hard to fix" argument is somewhat weaker in California's current political environment, though the amendment must be "consistent with and further the purposes" of the act, which constrains repeal of the tort provisions (arguably those further "building more middle-class housing"). Still, the legislature can't easily undo it.

Let me consider who the most credible analysts are:
- LAO: neutral, no direct costs, three big unknowns.
- PPIC (McGhee): could meaningfully help if targeted to lower-priced homes; but affordability is the binding constraint for most.
- CA YIMBY: neutral — "If we are going to subsidize demand for homes, this is one of the better ways to do it. However, given the ongoing shortage, such subsidies are unlikely to reduce costs."
- CA Budget & Policy Center: skeptical — "It's not guaranteed"; monthly repayment erodes benefit; equity concerns; sprawl; could have been done legislatively.
- LWVC: NO.
- HJTA: NO.
- Hoover: balanced, flags risks.
- SPUR: YES.
- Editorial boards: split. SF Chronicle YES; Sac Bee YES; Bay Area News Group NO; SDUT NO; OC Register NO; Press-Enterprise NO.

So among organizations with actual policy analysis (rather than interest), the left-of-center housing/budget experts are skeptical-to-opposed, the YIMBYs are neutral, and the pro-housing urbanist group SPUR supports. Interest groups (realtors, builders, carpenters) support.

Given the target of the question — "is it better to vote yes or no" — I should form a judgment. I lean NO, for these decisive reasons:

1. The benefit is speculative while the costs are concrete. The program's value depends entirely on investors buying taxable, non-recourse second-lien bonds at below-market rates — which no one has committed to. If rates are market-level (>7%), the second mortgage adds ~$900–$1,000+/month, which defeats the purpose for most households (PPIC: fewer than 40% of eligible renters could afford even an entry-level new home with the down payment solved).

2. Even in the best case, it mostly subsidizes higher-income buyers. 200% AMI = up to ~$400k for a family of four in SF/Santa Clara, on homes up to $1.56M, with no first-time-buyer requirement and no shared-appreciation recapture. Existing CalHFA programs (MyHome, Dream For All) are better targeted and use deferred/silent seconds that don't compete with the monthly budget. Prop 37 is a step backward in design.

3. In a supply-constrained market, demand subsidies get capitalized into prices — CA YIMBY, AEI, and standard economics agree. The likely winners are builders and realtors, who wrote and funded the measure ($33.6M, ~70% from CAR/NAR) and who secured a provision requiring every borrower to retain a licensed real estate agent — a guaranteed commission.

4. It permanently weakens homeowner legal protections in ways the ballot title, summary, and pro argument never mention: a 30% cap on contingency fees for construction-defect cases on any qualified new home; allowing builders to obtain releases in exchange for repairs (which Civil Code §926 currently prohibits); a dismissal motion if homeowners don't act within 120 days; and exemption of these second liens from Civil Code §2924.13's 2025 foreclosure protections. Plus program rules are exempt from the APA. These changes take effect whether or not a single bond is ever sold.

5. It loads households with 100% financing (3% cash + 17% second + 80% first) plus HOA dues (~70% of new homes), Mello-Roos assessments, and California's dysfunctional insurance market — the classic setup for underwater borrowers and second-lien losses in a downturn, with predictable political pressure for a state backstop despite the non-recourse language.

6. There's no reason to do this by initiative: revenue bonds don't need voter approval. The legislature or CalHFA could create a properly targeted version — first-time/first-generation buyers, deferred-payment structure, infill priority, no tort giveaways — without permanently embedding it in a statute amendable only by a 60% vote.

Counterweight acknowledged: no General Fund cost, real consumer protections on loan terms, new-construction targeting, and strong broad support. But on balance, the "no" case is stronger.

Hmm, let me double-check one thing: is the 30% contingency fee cap applicable to all "qualified new homes" or only those built by qualified builders? Reading the text: Section 51515.04(e)(2): "Notwithstanding any other law, in any action brought by a homeowner or group of homeowners asserting claims subject to the procedures set forth in Chapter 4 ... and Chapter 5 ... of Title 7 ... of the Civil Code or the procedures set forth in subparagraph (B) of paragraph (1) of this subdivision related to a qualified new home, the maximum allowable attorney contingency fee shall not exceed 30 percent..." — yes, it applies to any qualified new home, whether or not built under the qualified builder option. And (e)(1)(A) says Title 7 applies to qualified new homes except as modified in (B) for qualified-builder homes. So the fee cap is broader. Confirmed. Note that 30% is not an unusual contingency cap (it's roughly standard for the pre-litigation stage), but it does apply regardless of complexity, subject to court approval for more. It's a moderate change, not draconian. Still, it's a tort-reform provision bundled in.

Also, the release/waiver provision (e)(1)(B)(iii) is limited to qualified-builder homes, and it requires the homeowner be satisfied, release be knowing and voluntary, and not extend to unaddressed defects. That's actually fairly protective in drafting — more so than the critics suggest. Hmm. That tempers my concern #4 somewhat. The LAO's letter notes current law prohibits builders from obtaining a release in exchange for repair work; Prop 37 allows it, but with conditions. That's a genuine reduction in homeowner leverage (a homeowner who accepts repairs signs away claims about those defects) but it's bounded.

Still, the 2924.13 exemption is unexplained and cuts against consumers, and the APA exemption reduces transparency.

Let me also weigh: how much does one vote matter? It's polling 65-32, so it'll pass regardless. The question asks which is "better," so I should give my honest substantive judgment.

Let me do one more check: are there any reputable analyses suggesting the program would actually deliver below-market rates, e.g., has CalHFA or the campaign identified institutional investors? And is there anything about the requirement that the bonds qualify for CRA credit? Also let me verify the Sacramento Bee's YES reasoning and the SF Chronicle's YES reasoning, to steelman.

Actually, let me check one more important thing: whether there's any risk to CalHFA's existing programs or the state's credit rating, and whether CalHFA's board officially supports it. Also check the "Building a Better California" involvement (Brin/Doerr — they also fund No on 40 billionaire tax), which suggests a political trade. And California Forever's $50k (Solano new town developer — benefits from greenfield demand subsidy). These support the "interest-driven" critique.

I think I have enough. Let me do one final check on the pro-side steelman (SF Chronicle / Sac Bee editorials) to make sure I'm not missing a compelling argument.","format":"unknown","index":0}]

The SF Chronicle board's rationale is telling: "Its scope is limited enough that we don't think it will fundamentally change the state's housing landscape. But given how dire our housing crisis is, any positive impact is better than none at all." That's a weak endorsement — "low-risk experiment."

So the strongest yes case is: it costs taxpayers nothing, it's a low-risk experiment, and it might help. The strongest no case: it's a badly targeted demand subsidy that will likely be capitalized into higher new-home prices, benefiting builders and realtors who funded it, while saddling moderate-income buyers with a second mortgage at unknown (likely above-first-mortgage) rates; and it permanently weakens homeowner construction-defect and foreclosure protections with no guarantee the financing ever materializes.

Let me think about which is genuinely "better."

A key consideration: the option value / asymmetric downside. If the bonds don't sell or rates are too high, the program simply doesn't launch — no harm to taxpayers, no harm to borrowers (no one takes a loan they can't afford at rates that don't beat alternatives; borrowers are rational and CalHFA is required to keep rates as low as possible). So the "buyers get over-leveraged" concern is partly self-limiting: borrowers choose whether to participate, and they'd compare against PMI on a conventional 3%-down loan. Actually, that's a fair point — McClatchy noted proponents modeled that even at relatively high second-mortgage rates, buyers could still save money compared with private mortgage insurance. Hmm, is that right? PMI on a 97% LTV loan is typically 0.5–1.5% of loan amount annually, i.e., ~$500-900/month on a $640k loan early on, declining as equity builds. A 17% second mortgage at 7% over 30 years on $136k = ~$905/month. So it's roughly comparable in early years but doesn't decline/cancel like PMI does... Actually PMI cancels at 78% LTV, whereas the second mortgage must be paid down. So it's not obviously better. But it also gives 20% equity upfront which means better first-mortgage rate (no high-LTV pricing) — could save on the first mortgage rate too. It's a wash-ish.

So the borrower harm is modest and voluntary. The real question is: does it accomplish a public good, or does it mostly transfer public credit capacity to builders/realtors while worsening affordability for non-participants and weakening homeowner legal rights?

Let's think about the price capitalization concern. New-home markets in California: builders price to what the market bears. Adding a financing option that lets buyers put 3% down instead of 20% expands the pool of qualified buyers for new homes → builders raise prices on those homes up to the cap. The cap is generous ($1.04M–$1.56M). So there's a real risk the subsidy is captured by builders — exactly what CA YIMBY and AEI predict, and what Carl DeMaio says ("developers would be the ones who truly benefit"). This is the standard finding in the economics literature on down-payment assistance in supply-constrained markets (e.g., Harris et al. AEI work showing DPA raises prices roughly dollar-for-dollar).

That's a substantive economic argument against. And the countervailing supply response — the qualified builder option + defect reform to unlock condo construction — is speculative and, per CA YIMBY, unlikely to be the binding constraint (permits for market-rate ownership units stayed flat 43k–55k even as prices spiked 2020–2022, indicating supply is constrained by regulation/land/costs, not demand).

Then there's the tort/consumer-protection trade. The defect-liability changes take effect for "qualified new homes" and "qualified builders" regardless of whether any bonds are sold. They reduce homeowner remedies (release in exchange for repairs, 120-day dismissal motion, 30% contingency cap, APA-exempt rules). They're permanent-ish (60% vote + purpose-consistency requirement). And the ballot materials barely disclosed them: the LAO analysis mentions "different construction defect rules, which generally aim to provide more flexibility to developers," but the title/summary and pro argument say nothing. That's a meaningful process defect.

Combined with:
- Funded ~70% by realtors (CAR/NAR ~$23M of $33.6M), who also secured a mandate that every borrower retain a licensed agent (guaranteed ~2-3% commission, paid by the seller but ultimately baked into prices);
- $6M from Building a Better California (Brin/Doerr), which is also the main funder of No on Prop 40 (billionaire tax) — suggesting a political package deal;
- $50k from California Forever, a greenfield new-town developer that directly benefits from a subsidy steering demand to sprawl;
- Income caps to 200% AMI (up to $401,600 for a family of four in SF), price caps to $1.56M, no first-time-buyer priority, no shared-appreciation recapture — i.e., much less progressive than existing CalHFA programs it sits alongside;
- Budget Center: it could have been enacted legislatively (revenue bonds need no voter approval), so bypassing the legislature was a choice to avoid negotiation/targeting.

Versus the yes case:
- Zero General Fund cost (real, and verified by LAO and the bond text's non-recourse language);
- Voluntary participation, fixed rate, fee caps, no prepayment penalty, cash-flow underwriting, mandatory buyer representation, education, annual audit;
- New-construction-only design at least avoids the pure musical-chairs problem of subsidizing existing homes;
- Broad support including Newsom, labor, veterans, SPUR, SF Chronicle, McClatchy;
- 65% polling — will pass anyway.

Weighing all this, I think the balance tips to NO. The decisive reasons:

1. The measure's central promise — "below-market, fixed-rate loans" — is not in the text and depends on an unproven philanthropic bond market. Absent that, second-lien rates above 7% make the program unaffordable for most of the people it claims to help (PPIC: 56% of renters can't afford an entry-level new home even with the down payment solved; <0.5% can afford the top of the price range), while adding a permanent second payment on top of HOA dues, Mello-Roos, and insurance costs.

2. In a supply-constrained market, a demand subsidy gets capitalized into prices. The most likely effect is higher prices on new homes up to the caps — a transfer to builders and realtors — not more affordability. CA YIMBY (the state's leading supply-side housing group) declined to support it for exactly this reason; permit data shows ownership-unit production was flat through the 2020–22 price spike, so demand isn't the binding constraint.

3. It's badly targeted: 200% AMI, $1.56M price caps, no first-time/first-generation priority, no equity recapture. Existing CalHFA programs do this better and with deferred-payment structures that don't compete with the family's monthly budget. Prop 37 is a less progressive use of $25B of state credit capacity than the programs already on the books — and it duplicates Prop 1's $1.1B homeownership allocation on the same ballot.

4. It permanently weakens homeowner legal protections — release-for-repair waivers (currently banned by Civil Code §926), 120-day dismissal motions, a 30% contingency-fee cap for all qualified new homes, exemption from Civil Code §2924.13 foreclosure protections, and rules exempt from the APA — with a >60% legislative vote required to amend. These take effect whether or not a single bond ever sells, and none of them were disclosed in the title, summary, or argument in favor.

5. The conflict of interest is stark: ~70% of the $33.6M came from realtors, plus Brin/Doerr's committee and a greenfield new-town developer; and the text mandates that every borrower retain a licensed real estate agent — a guaranteed commission for the measure's chief funder.

So: no.

Actually, let me pause. Am I being too harsh? The "no cost to taxpayers, low-risk experiment" argument is genuinely strong, and the SF Chronicle/CalMatters framing ("low-risk radical experiment") is persuasive. If the downside is truly near zero, why not yes?

But the downside isn't zero:
- The tort-law changes are certain and permanent.
- The sprawl steering is a real policy harm (Budget Center, LWVC) — subsidizing exclusively new construction with no infill/jobs-housing/transit proximity requirement, in a state with climate and VMT goals, and specifically benefiting greenfield developers.
- The price capitalization harms non-participant buyers of new homes and renters indirectly.
- The over-leverage risk to participating households is real (3% skin in the game, 100% LTV).
- It consumes CalHFA's administrative capacity and crowds out better-targeted programs.

And there's a strong "do it right instead" alternative: the legislature/CalHFA can issue revenue bonds without voter approval, with first-time-buyer targeting, deferred/silent-second structure, infill priority, and no tort giveaways. Voting no doesn't kill the idea; it sends it back to a forum where it can be properly designed.

I'm comfortable: no.

Let me quickly check if there's any analysis showing the program would produce below-market rates credibly, or any new information (e.g., commitments from foundations). And check if any consumer/homeowner groups (e.g., Consumer Watchdog, Consumer Federation of California) took a position. Let me do one more search round.

Existing CalHFA programs do this better and with deferred-payment structures that don't compete with the family's monthly budget. Prop 37 is a less progressive use of $25B of state credit capacity than the programs already on the books — and it duplicates Prop 1's $1.1B homeownership allocation on the same ballot.

4. It permanently weakens homeowner legal protections — release-for-repair waivers (currently banned by Civil Code §926), 120-day dismissal motions, a 30% contingency-fee cap for all qualified new homes, exemption from Civil Code §2924.13 foreclosure protections, and rules exempt from the APA — with a >60% legislative vote required to amend. These take effect whether or not a single bond ever sells, and none of them were disclosed in the title, summary, or argument in favor.

5. The conflict of interest is stark: ~70% of the $33.6M came from realtors, plus Brin/Doerr's committee and a greenfield new-town developer; and the text mandates that every borrower retain a licensed real estate agent — a guaranteed commission for the measure's chief funder.

So: no.

Actually, let me pause. Am I being too harsh? The "no cost to taxpayers, low-risk experiment" argument is genuinely strong, and the SF Chronicle/CalMatters framing ("low-risk radical experiment") is persuasive. If the downside is truly near zero, why not yes?

But the downside isn't zero:
- The tort-law changes are certain and permanent.
- The sprawl steering is a real policy harm (Budget Center, LWVC) — subsidizing exclusively new construction with no infill/jobs-housing/transit proximity requirement, in a state with climate and VMT goals, and specifically benefiting greenfield developers.
- The price capitalization harms non-participant buyers of new homes and renters indirectly.
- The over-leverage risk to participating households is real (3% skin in the game, 100% LTV).
- It consumes CalHFA's administrative capacity and crowds out better-targeted programs.

And there's a strong "do it right instead" alternative: the legislature/CalHFA can issue revenue bonds without voter approval, with first-time-buyer targeting, deferred/silent-second structure, infill priority, and no tort giveaways. Voting no doesn't kill the idea; it sends it back to a forum where it can be properly designed.

I'm comfortable: no.

content.thinking:
The SF Chronicle board's rationale is telling: "Its scope is limited enough that we don't think it will fundamentally change the state's housing landscape. But given how dire our housing crisis is, any positive impact is better than none at all." That's a weak endorsement — "low-risk experiment."

So the strongest yes case is: it costs taxpayers nothing, it's a low-risk experiment, and it might help. The strongest no case: it's a badly targeted demand subsidy that will likely be capitalized into higher new-home prices, benefiting builders and realtors who funded it, while saddling moderate-income buyers with a second mortgage at unknown (likely above-first-mortgage) rates; and it permanently weakens homeowner construction-defect and foreclosure protections with no guarantee the financing ever materializes.

Let me think about which is genuinely "better."

A key consideration: the option value / asymmetric downside. If the bonds don't sell or rates are too high, the program simply doesn't launch — no harm to taxpayers, no harm to borrowers (no one takes a loan they can't afford at rates that don't beat alternatives; borrowers are rational and CalHFA is required to keep rates as low as possible). So the "buyers get over-leveraged" concern is partly self-limiting: borrowers choose whether to participate, and they'd compare against PMI on a conventional 3%-down loan. Actually, that's a fair point — McClatchy noted proponents modeled that even at relatively high second-mortgage rates, buyers could still save money compared with private mortgage insurance. Hmm, is that right? PMI on a 97% LTV loan is typically 0.5–1.5% of loan amount annually, i.e., ~$500-900/month on a $640k loan early on, declining as equity builds. A 17% second mortgage at 7% over 30 years on $136k = ~$905/month. So it's roughly comparable in early years but doesn't decline/cancel like PMI does... Actually PMI cancels at 78% LTV, whereas the second mortgage must be paid down. So it's not obviously better. But it also gives 20% equity upfront which means better first-mortgage rate (no high-LTV pricing) — could save on the first mortgage rate too. It's a wash-ish.

So the borrower harm is modest and voluntary. The real question is: does it accomplish a public good, or does it mostly transfer public credit capacity to builders/realtors while worsening affordability for non-participants and weakening homeowner legal rights?

Let's think about the price capitalization concern. New-home markets in California: builders price to what the market bears. Adding a financing option that lets buyers put 3% down instead of 20% expands the pool of qualified buyers for new homes → builders raise prices on those homes up to the cap. The cap is generous ($1.04M–$1.56M). So there's a real risk the subsidy is captured by builders — exactly what CA YIMBY and AEI predict, and what Carl DeMaio says ("developers would be the ones who truly benefit"). This is the standard finding in the economics literature on down-payment assistance in supply-constrained markets (e.g., Harris et al. AEI work showing DPA raises prices roughly dollar-for-dollar).

That's a substantive economic argument against. And the countervailing supply response — the qualified builder option + defect reform to unlock condo construction — is speculative and, per CA YIMBY, unlikely to be the binding constraint (permits for market-rate ownership units stayed flat 43k–55k even as prices spiked 2020–2022, indicating supply is constrained by regulation/land/costs, not demand).

Then there's the tort/consumer-protection trade. The defect-liability changes take effect for "qualified new homes" and "qualified builders" regardless of whether any bonds are sold. They reduce homeowner remedies (release in exchange for repairs, 120-day dismissal motion, 30% contingency cap, APA-exempt rules). They're permanent-ish (60% vote + purpose-consistency requirement). And the ballot materials barely disclosed them: the LAO analysis mentions "different construction defect rules, which generally aim to provide more flexibility to developers," but the title/summary and pro argument say nothing. That's a meaningful process defect.

Combined with:
- Funded ~70% by realtors (CAR/NAR ~$23M of $33.6M), who also secured a mandate that every borrower retain a licensed agent (guaranteed ~2-3% commission, paid by the seller but ultimately baked into prices);
- $6M from Building a Better California (Brin/Doerr), which is also the main funder of No on Prop 40 (billionaire tax) — suggesting a political package deal;
- $50k from California Forever, a greenfield new-town developer that directly benefits from a subsidy steering demand to sprawl;
- Income caps to 200% AMI (up to $401,600 for a family of four in SF), price caps to $1.56M, no first-time-buyer priority, no shared-appreciation recapture — i.e., much less progressive than existing CalHFA programs it sits alongside;
- Budget Center: it could have been enacted legislatively (revenue bonds need no voter approval), so bypassing the legislature was a choice to avoid negotiation/targeting.

Versus the yes case:
- Zero General Fund cost (real, and verified by LAO and the bond text's non-recourse language);
- Voluntary participation, fixed rate, fee caps, no prepayment penalty, cash-flow underwriting, mandatory buyer representation, education, annual audit;
- New-construction-only design at least avoids the pure musical-chairs problem of subsidizing existing homes;
- Broad support including Newsom, labor, veterans, SPUR, SF Chronicle, McClatchy;
- 65% polling — will pass anyway.

Weighing all this, I think the balance tips to NO. The decisive reasons:

1. The measure's central promise — "below-market, fixed-rate loans" — is not in the text and depends on an unproven philanthropic bond market. Absent that, second-lien rates above 7% make the program unaffordable for most of the people it claims to help (PPIC: 56% of renters can't afford an entry-level new home even with the down payment solved; <0.5% can afford the top of the price range), while adding a permanent second payment on top of HOA dues, Mello-Roos, and insurance costs.

2. In a supply-constrained market, a demand subsidy gets capitalized into prices. The most likely effect is higher prices on new homes up to the caps — a transfer to builders and realtors — not more affordability. CA YIMBY (the state's leading supply-side housing group) declined to support it for exactly this reason; permit data shows ownership-unit production was flat through the 2020–22 price spike, so demand isn't the binding constraint.

3. It's badly targeted: 200% AMI, $1.56M price caps, no first-time/first-generation priority, no equity recapture. Existing CalHFA programs do this better and with deferred-payment structures that don't compete with the family's monthly budget. Prop 37 is a less progressive use of $25B of state credit capacity than the programs already on the books — and it duplicates Prop 1's $1.1B homeownership allocation on the same ballot.

4. It permanently weakens homeowner legal protections — release-for-repair waivers (currently banned by Civil Code §926), 120-day dismissal motions, a 30% contingency-fee cap for all qualified new homes, exemption from Civil Code §2924.13 foreclosure protections, and rules exempt from the APA — with a >60% legislative vote required to amend. These take effect whether or not a single bond ever sells, and none of them were disclosed in the title, summary, or argument in favor.

5. The conflict of interest is stark: ~70% of the $33.6M came from realtors, plus Brin/Doerr's committee and a greenfield new-town developer; and the text mandates that every borrower retain a licensed real estate agent — a guaranteed commission for the measure's chief funder.

So: no.

Actually, let me pause. Am I being too harsh? The "no cost to taxpayers, low-risk experiment" argument is genuinely strong, and the SF Chronicle/CalMatters framing ("low-risk radical experiment") is persuasive. If the downside is truly near zero, why not yes?

But the downside isn't zero:
- The tort-law changes are certain and permanent.
- The sprawl steering is a real policy harm (Budget Center, LWVC) — subsidizing exclusively new construction with no infill/jobs-housing/transit proximity requirement, in a state with climate and VMT goals, and specifically benefiting greenfield developers.
- The price capitalization harms non-participant buyers of new homes and renters indirectly.
- The over-leverage risk to participating households is real (3% skin in the game, 100% LTV).
- It consumes CalHFA's administrative capacity and crowds out better-targeted programs.

And there's a strong "do it right instead" alternative: the legislature/CalHFA can issue revenue bonds without voter approval, with first-time-buyer targeting, deferred/silent-second structure, infill priority, and no tort giveaways. Voting no doesn't kill the idea; it sends it back to a forum where it can be properly designed.

I'm comfortable: no.

Let me make sure I'm not missing anything that would flip me. Let me quickly check if there's any analysis showing the program would produce below-market rates credibly, or any new information (e.g., commitments from foundations). And check if any consumer/homeowner groups (e.g., Consumer Watchdog, Consumer Federation of California) took a position. Let me do one more search round.

I have comprehensive research. Now let me make the final decision.

Summary of the case:

FOR YES:
- LAO: no direct state/local cost; bonds are non-recourse revenue bonds explicitly not a pledge of state faith and credit.
- Voluntary participation; consumer protections (fixed rate, no prepayment penalty, fee caps, cash-flow underwriting, mandatory buyer representation, homeowner education, independent annual audit).
- Tied exclusively to new construction — at least attempts to add supply, unlike generic DPA.
- Could help up to ~560,000 buyers (PPIC central estimate), closing ~41% of CA's homeownership gap in the best case.
- Broad support: Newsom, Becerra, CA Democratic Party, carpenters/nurses unions, veterans groups, chambers, builders, realtors, SPUR, Grow SF, Consumer Watchdog, SF Chronicle, McClatchy/Sac Bee, SD Taxpayers.
- Polling: 65% yes / 32% no.
- Downside to the public fisc is limited; "if it doesn't work, the state's not really on the hook" (CA Budget Center's Chris Hoene).

FOR NO:
- The promised "below-market" rates are not in the text and depend on an unverified philanthropic bond market; Hertzberg won't name any committed investors. Second-lien, taxable, non-recourse bonds will price above first-mortgage rates (>7% now). At 7%, a $136k second mortgage on an $800k home ≈ $900+/month extra. PPIC: 56% of renters couldn't afford an entry-level new home even with the down payment solved; <0.5% could afford homes at the top of the price range. So the program may deliver little.
- Badly targeted: 200% AMI (up to ~$401,600 for a family of four in SF/Santa Clara), price caps to $1.56M, no first-time/first-generation priority, no shared-appreciation recapture. Worse-designed than existing CalHFA MyHome/Dream For All (deferred silent seconds, income limits, appreciation share). Budget Center + LWVC: likely to widen racial/economic gaps, benefiting white/Asian and higher-income households.
- Demand subsidy in a supply-constrained market → capitalized into prices. CA YIMBY (the leading pro-housing supply group) declined to support: "there is no shortage of buyers for newly built ownership housing"; permits flat 43k–55k through the 2020–22 price spike shows demand isn't the binding constraint. AEI's Pinto agrees. Winners = builders/sellers/realtors.
- Permanently weakens homeowner protections, undisclosed in the title/summary/pro argument: 30% contingency-fee cap for construction-defect actions on ANY qualified new home; builders may obtain releases in exchange for repairs (Civil Code §926 currently prohibits this); motion to dismiss if homeowner doesn't act within 120 days; exemption from Civil Code §2924.13 (2025 dormant-second-lien foreclosure protections); program rules exempt from the APA; amendable only by >60% of each house. These take effect whether or not a single bond is ever sold.
- Sprawl: exclusive new-construction requirement with no infill/jobs/transit proximity requirement, steering demand to greenfield/exurban areas (Budget Center, LWVC), with HOA dues (~70% of new homes), Mello-Roos assessments, and CA's insurance crisis layered on top. New-town developer California Forever contributed.
- Over-leverage: 3% own cash + 17% second + 80% first = 100% financing; small equity cushion; second lien takes losses first in a downturn. HJTA warns of mass foreclosures; political pressure for a state backstop is a real moral-obligation risk (Hoover, McClatchy).
- Conflict of interest: $35M raised, ~$23–25M from CAR/NAR realtor committees, $6M from Brin/Doerr's Building a Better California (also the main funder of No on Prop 40), plus carpenters' unions and California Forever. And §51515.04(c) requires every borrower to retain a licensed California real estate agent/broker — a guaranteed commission for the chief funder.
- Unnecessary via initiative: revenue bonds need no voter approval; the legislature/CalHFA could do this with proper targeting and without tort giveaways. Voting no sends it back to be drafted properly.
- Endorsement split: Bay Area News Group (Mercury News/East Bay Times), OC Register, Press-Enterprise, San Diego Union-Tribune = NO; LWVC, HJTA, Reform California/DeMaio = NO; SPUR, SF Chronicle, McClatchy, Consumer Watchdog = YES.

Deciding factor: The benefits are speculative and conditional on a philanthropic bond market that no one has confirmed, while the costs are concrete, immediate, and permanent — a poorly targeted subsidy likely captured by builders and realtors (who wrote and funded it and secured a mandatory-agent commission), higher prices for new homes, weaker homeowner construction-defect and foreclosure remedies locked in behind a 60% amendment threshold, and more household leverage. And there is a strictly better alternative: CalHFA/legislature can issue revenue bonds without voter approval and design a targeted version (first-time/first-gen buyers, deferred silent seconds, infill priority, no tort concessions).

Final answer: no.

I have comprehensive research. Now let me make the final decision.

Summary of the case:

FOR YES:
- LAO: no direct state/local cost; bonds are non-recourse revenue bonds explicitly not a pledge of state faith and credit.
- Voluntary participation; consumer protections (fixed rate, no prepayment penalty, fee caps, cash-flow underwriting, mandatory buyer representation, homeowner education, independent annual audit).
- Tied exclusively to new construction — at least attempts to add supply, unlike generic DPA.
- Could help up to ~560,000 buyers (PPIC central estimate), closing ~41% of CA's homeownership gap in the best case.
- Broad support: Newsom, Becerra, CA Democratic Party, carpenters/nurses unions, veterans groups, chambers, builders, realtors, SPUR, Grow SF, Consumer Watchdog, SF Chronicle, McClatchy/Sac Bee, SD Taxpayers.
- Polling: 65% yes / 32% no.
- Downside to the public fisc is limited; "if it doesn't work, the state's not really on the hook" (CA Budget Center's Chris Hoene).

FOR NO:
- The promised "below-market" rates are not in the text and depend on an unverified philanthropic bond market; Hertzberg won't name any committed investors. Second-lien, taxable, non-recourse bonds will price above first-mortgage rates (>7% now). At 7%, a $136k second mortgage on an $800k home ≈ $900+/month extra. PPIC: 56% of renters couldn't afford an entry-level new home even with the down payment solved; <0.5% could afford homes at the top of the price range. So the program may deliver little.
- Badly targeted: 200% AMI (up to ~$401,600 for a family of four in SF/Santa Clara), price caps to $1.56M, no first-time/first-generation priority, no shared-appreciation recapture. Worse-designed than existing CalHFA MyHome/Dream For All (deferred silent seconds, income limits, appreciation share). Budget Center + LWVC: likely to widen racial/economic gaps, benefiting white/Asian and higher-income households.
- Demand subsidy in a supply-constrained market → capitalized into prices. CA YIMBY (the leading pro-housing supply group) declined to support: "there is no shortage of buyers for newly built ownership housing"; permits flat 43k–55k through the 2020–22 price spike shows demand isn't the binding constraint. AEI's Pinto agrees. Winners = builders/sellers/realtors.
- Permanently weakens homeowner protections, undisclosed in the title/summary/pro argument: 30% contingency-fee cap for construction-defect actions on ANY qualified new home; builders may obtain releases in exchange for repairs (Civil Code §926 currently prohibits this); motion to dismiss if homeowner doesn't act within 120 days; exemption from Civil Code §2924.13 (2025 dormant-second-lien foreclosure protections); program rules exempt from the APA; amendable only by >60% of each house. These take effect whether or not a single bond is ever sold.
- Sprawl: exclusive new-construction requirement with no infill/jobs/transit proximity requirement, steering demand to greenfield/exurban areas (Budget Center, LWVC), with HOA dues (~70% of new homes), Mello-Roos assessments, and CA's insurance crisis layered on top. New-town developer California Forever contributed.
- Over-leverage: 3% own cash + 17% second + 80% first = 100% financing; small equity cushion; second lien takes losses first in a downturn. HJTA warns of mass foreclosures; political pressure for a state backstop is a real moral-obligation risk (Hoover, McClatchy).
- Conflict of interest: $35M raised, ~$23–25M from CAR/NAR realtor committees, $6M from Brin/Doerr's Building a Better California (also the main funder of No on Prop 40), plus carpenters' unions and California Forever. And §51515.04(c) requires every borrower to retain a licensed California real estate agent/broker — a guaranteed commission for the chief funder.
- Unnecessary via initiative: revenue bonds need no voter approval; the legislature/CalHFA could do this with proper targeting and without tort giveaways. Voting no sends it back to be drafted properly.
- Endorsement split: Bay Area News Group (Mercury News/East Bay Times), OC Register, Press-Enterprise, San Diego Union-Tribune = NO; LWVC, HJTA, Reform California/DeMaio = NO; SPUR, SF Chronicle, McClatchy, Consumer Watchdog = YES.

Deciding factor: The benefits are speculative and conditional on a philanthropic bond market that no one has confirmed, while the costs are concrete, immediate, and permanent — a poorly targeted subsidy likely captured by builders and realtors (who wrote and funded it and secured a mandatory-agent commission), higher prices for new homes, weaker homeowner construction-defect and foreclosure remedies locked in behind a 60% amendment threshold, and more household leverage. And there is a strictly better alternative: CalHFA/legislature can issue revenue bonds without voter approval and design a targeted version (first-time/first-gen buyers, deferred silent seconds, infill priority, no tort concessions).

Final answer: no.

PROP
37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State. Fiscal Impact: No direct state or local costs. Supporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners’ payments on their home loans.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Zero Taxpayer Cost-No Taxpayer Risk. Prop. 37 makes buying a home more affordable, keeping homeownership attainable for hardworking and middle-class Californians, with low-interest mortgages funded by private bond investors, NOT TAXPAYERS. Must be CA resident to qualify, meet income requirements, occupy home, make monthly payments, repay loan. Strict accountability/audits.
CON
NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 37 WAS SUBMITTED.

**Sacramento, Calif.** – Today California Secretary of State Shirley N. Weber, Ph.D., made the November 3, 2026, California General Election Official Voter Information Guide available for public review.
The guide, which will be mailed to every voting household in California, includes information about propositions and statements from candidates running for constitutional offices, as well as other important election information such as the California Voter Bill of Rights and information about how eligible Californians can vote.
California’s Official Voter Information Guide is available in 10 languages—English, Spanish, Chinese, Hindi, Japanese, Khmer, Korean, Tagalog, Thai, and Vietnamese.
The guide is available for public examination from July 21, 2026 through August 10, 2026 at https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/public-display and at the Office of the Secretary of State’s Sacramento and Los Angeles locations.
During this public display period, any elector can challenge any portion of the Official Voter Information Guide in Sacramento Superior Court.
Following the conclusion of the public examination period, the Office of the Secretary of State will begin printing and mailing the statewide Voter Information Guide to all households that have at least one registered voter.

PROP
37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
State Revenue Bonds. Bonds are a way that governments borrow money, most commonly for public projects such as schools or bridges. The state sells bonds to investors to receive up-front funding for these projects. Over time, investors are repaid with interest. The state sells two main types of bonds: general obligation bonds and revenue bonds. The state usually repays general obligation bonds using the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) In contrast, revenue bonds are repaid using revenue from fees or other payments by the users of the project (such as from bridge tolls).
Some People Seek Down Payment Assistance. When purchasing a home, most people pay some of the cost up front-typically 3 percent to 20 percent of the home price. The up-front payment is known as a down payment. If people cannot afford the down payment, there are different government programs available to provide down payment assistance to eligible homebuyers. To cover the remaining cost of the home, homebuyers get a loan, called a mortgage. Homebuyers then pay off the mortgage by making monthly payments that include interest.
California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA). CalHFA is a state entity that administers programs designed to help low- and moderate-income Californians afford housing. CalHFA has a few programs that provide down payment assistance to homebuyers. The down payment assistance programs are loans that must be repaid under certain terms and conditions.
Construction Defect Law. To try to prevent construction defects, state law sets minimum standards that builders must follow for new residential construction. Current law also establishes a process that homeowners and housing builders must follow before a homeowner is able to sue a builder for alleged violations of those minimum standards. For example, the homeowner must provide notice to the builder that includes certain information concerning a claim of construction defect.
PROPOSAL
Revenue Bond to Pay for a New Down Payment Assistance Program. Proposition 37 allows CalHFA to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. CalHFA would use the bond funds to create a down payment assistance program called the “middle-class homeownership loan.” Each loan would cover up to 17 percent of the home price. (Homebuyers would need to provide a down payment of at least 3 percent of the home price.) Homeowners’ monthly payments on their loan would be designed to repay the bonds over time and cover the program’s administrative costs. CalHFA also would be required to keep interest costs for homebuyers as low as possible. CalHFA would decide how much of the bonds to issue (up to $25 billion) and over what time period.
Buyers and Homes Must Meet Certain Requirements. To participate in a middleclass homeownership loan, people and homes would need to meet certain requirements. For example, an applicant would need to be a resident of the state and have a household income no more than double the typical income level in their area. For a home to be eligible for purchase through the program, among other requirements, the buyer would need to be the first purchaser of the home and the price could not exceed certain limits.
Housing Developer Options. Under Proposition 37, all developers could build homes eligible for purchase under the program. Developers also could choose to participate in a “qualified builder option.” Developers that chose this option would be required to meet higher labor standards, such as using workers with a certain type of training for certain types of housing projects. In exchange, developers would be subject to different construction defect rules, which generally aim to provide more flexibility to developers.
FISCAL EFFECTS
No Direct State or Local Costs. Because Proposition 37 uses the payments from homebuyers to repay bond investors, it would not result in direct state or local costs.
Other Potential Effects. A number of factors, which are unknown at this time, could affect Proposition 37’s scope and impact. These include (1) the extent to which investors want to buy the bond, (2) how much the loans available under this proposed program cost homebuyers compared with other down payment assistance options, and (3) whether the program results in increased home construction and homebuying.

Prop. 37 explained: Can a $25 billion bond make homeownership in California attainable?
by
Ben Christopher (https://calmatters.org/author/ben-christopher/)

In summary
A clever solution or a confusing gimmick? Like it or hate it, almost everyone has questions about Proposition 37. Here are a few of the big ones — with the best available answers.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
It’s a bond, but not like any other bond on the ballot.
It promises to provide homebuyers with mortgages, but not your typical mortgages.
It would set up a down payment assistance program, but one unlike any other in the country.
There are plenty of consequential and controversial propositions (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/) on California’s ballot this year, but none as plainly weird as Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/).
Supporters call it an “elegant” solution to the fact that so many Californians can’t afford to buy a home. Detractors characterize it as a Rube Goldberg-esque gimmick (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/02/endorsements-props-2-37-wouldnt-yield-saner-state-budgets-more-housing/?clearUserState=true) that’s too clever by half. Virtually everyone, including some hired to analyze the proposition, has questions.
Here are a few of the big ones — with the best available answers.
Q: What would Proposition 37 do?
A: If it passes, the state would be able to borrow up to $25 billion to set up a new loan program to help people afford down payments on new home purchases.
$25 billion ? With a “B”? That’s a lot of money, even for a state with a $352 billion budget (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-gavin-newsom-final-budget-deal/) .
It is. But unlike other bonds on the ballot, this isn’t supposed to cost the state anything.
When the state sells bonds, it’s borrowing money. Most bonds, like Propositions 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) and 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/), would be paid back directly with tax dollars.
With Prop. 37, the state would act more like a loan broker. The California Housing Finance Agency would borrow the money from private lenders (by selling them bonds) and then re-lend that money to homebuyers. When the homebuyers repay those loans, the money would go back to the bond holders with interest.

If homebuyers don’t make their payments, the private lenders would be left holding the bag, not state taxpayers. That’s according to the text of the measure, anyway, though some analysts (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-37#:~:text=But%20a,period) have expressed doubt that state lawmakers could resist the political pressure to bail out homebuyers in the event of a wave of defaults.
Are these loans just home mortgages?
Second mortgages, specifically.
Buyers would still have to purchase a house the old fashioned way, by going to a bank or broker and taking out a mortgage that covers the bulk of the home price. But that still leaves a down payment. The median down payment in California is 20%, according to the California Association of Realtors — though it tends to be lower for first-time buyers. For an $800,000 home, that’s $160,000.
That’s a lot! Is this second mortgage meant to cover the entire down payment?
Almost all of it.
The program would allow these loans to cover as much as 17% of a home’s value, reducing the $160,000 to $24,000.
Is helping people take on more debt when they buy a home a good thing?
Homeownership is hopelessly out of reach for many Californians, even those who might otherwise be considered comfortably middle class. California has either the second-lowest (https://www.census.gov/housing/hvs/data/rates.html) or lowest (https://www.minneapolisfed.org/community-development-and-engagement/data-and-resources/homeowners-to-population-data) homeownership rate of any state, depending on how you measure it.
For many Californians stuck renting, high monthly mortgage payments — reliably higher (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/12/homeownership-vs-renting/) than a typical rent across much of the state — make homebuying a no-go. For anyone in that situation, tacking on a second mortgage with another monthly payment isn’t going to help.
But for some, it’s the size of the down payment that keeps homeownership out of reach. Roughly 40% of recent buyers turned to friends or family to help bridge this financial gap, according to a national survey (https://www.lendingtree.com/home/mortgage/down-payment-help-survey/#more-than-1-in-3-who-received-help-say-they-couldnt-have-bought-their-home-without-it). The gap is especially large in California, where home values are so high.
Asking a family to squirrel that much away is like asking them to “travel to the moon in a cardboard rocket ship,” Bob Hertzberg said in an interview.
Funny metaphor, but who is Bob Hertzberg?
He’s the former Speaker of the state Assembly, the former Senate majority leader, an active wheeler dealer in a wide variety of contemporary California (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-forever-solano-shipyard-deal/#:~:text=former%20Senate%20Majority%20Leader%20Bob%20Hertzberg) political (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-09-10/measure-ula-bill#:~:text=Bob%20Hertzberg) debates and Prop. 37’s singularly energetic author and hypeman.
Hertzberg has been working on this idea for years, along with the California Association of Realtors, and he says he’s come up with an admittedly unusual, but very “elegant” solution for middle-class renters unable to scrounge together a down payment.
If this passes, would I be able to get one of these loans?
If you’re a typical Californian, it’s quite likely you’d at least be eligible.
Under this program, anyone making less than double their county’s typical income qualifies, which ranges from roughly $116,000 in Imperial to just over $410,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. That covers roughly 90% of all renters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37?utm_source=ppic&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=blog_subscriber), according to a recent Public Policy Institute of California analysis.
Hertzberg and other supporters think it’s a good thing that such a wide swath of California would qualify.
There are plenty of existing down payment assistance programs aimed at helping lower income (https://www.bankrate.com/mortgages/what-is-an-fha-loan/), first-generation (https://calmatters.org/california-divide/2024/01/dream-for-all-california/) or veteran (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans) homebuyers, but Hertzberg argues that the broadly defined middle class needs help. Plus, the minimal qualifications will make it relatively light on red tape, he said.
But some opponents, like the League of Women Voters of California (https://lwvc.org/ballot-recommendations/), worry that offering a potential boost to so many would-be buyers will mean those who need help the least — people shy of the income cap, endowed with considerable wealth or able to borrow from family — will be the most likely to get the loans.
That, they warn, will only re-enforce the state’s existing economic and racial disparities (https://www.ppic.org/publication/wealth-in-california/).
What kind of house could a borrower get with one of these second mortgages?
Two conditions apply.
First, there’s a price cap. This gets a little technical, but basically the home has to be less than about $1 million in inland California and up to $1.5 million in Los Angeles, Orange County and the Bay Area.
Second, the home has to be newly built or newly converted into housing. In other words, the borrower has to be its first occupant. No re-sales.
